Appendix.title: Additive energy and approximate structure
Appendix.Content: Additive energy and approximate structure
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Additive energy measures how often two pairs from a set have the same sum: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>E</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>A</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>c</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>∈</mo> <msup> <mi>A</mi> <mn>4</mn> </msup> <mo>:</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>c</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </math>. A random-like set has relatively few repeated sums; a set with many additive coincidences often contains a structured subset. The Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers principle turns high energy into a large subset with small doubling, while Ruzsa-style inequalities and Freiman-type theorems describe how small doubling constrains approximate additive structure. In finite fields, sum-product results show that a set cannot remain simultaneously additively and multiplicatively concentrated unless it has special algebraic structure, such as subfield behavior. These implications are quantitative and depend on group or field hypotheses, subset size, and constants. High energy does not mean the entire set is a subgroup, and a small-doubling conclusion may apply only after discarding many elements. Energy is a counting diagnostic that guides structure theorems, not a complete classification by itself.

Appendix.title: Antialiasing and sample allocation
Appendix.Content: Antialiasing and sample allocation
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

SSAA increases spatial observations; MSAA principally adds coverage-related sampling under its shading conventions. TAA reuses aligned temporal observations. Nonlinear shading makes pre-/post-filtering noncommutative, so coarse rates need appropriate input/output policies.
Phase 9–10 development

Antialiasing combines a sampling pattern with a reconstruction or integration footprint so unresolved variation contributes with controlled error. More samples can reduce Monte Carlo variance, while better placement can reduce structured error; these are different effects. Adaptive allocation based on observed samples changes the sampling procedure and can affect uncertainty estimates. Spatial sample allocation should remain distinct from importance sampling over path or event space.

Appendix.title: Attention and visual transformers
Appendix.Content: Attention and visual transformers
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Self-attention lets each token build a context-dependent mixture of other tokens. A learned linear map produces queries <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>Q</mi> </math>, keys <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>K</mi> </math>, and values <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>V</mi> </math>; scaled dot products compare each query with all keys, softmax converts scores to weights, and those weights combine values. Multiple heads learn different relationships, while positional information tells the model where patches or words came from. Vision transformers split an image into patches, embed them as tokens, and process the sequence with attention and feed-forward blocks. Unlike a small convolution, global attention can relate distant regions in one layer, but its pairwise score matrix grows roughly as the square of token count. Patch size trades spatial detail for compute; positional encodings and training data affect transfer. Attention weights are a mechanism for mixing information, not an explanation of causal importance. A transformer still needs a task objective, data, optimization, and validation, and can fail under distribution shift or poor spatial grounding.

Appendix.title: Bounding volume hierarchies
Appendix.Content: Bounding volume hierarchies
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) organizes primitives into a tree of enclosing boxes. An internal node’s box contains the boxes of its children; a leaf stores a small set of triangles. To trace a ray, test the root box, recurse only into intersected children, and compare triangle hits in reached leaves. A box miss safely rejects every primitive beneath it, so the hierarchy reduces expensive exact tests when geometry is spatially coherent. Construction chooses how to group primitives and where to split; a surface-area heuristic estimates expected traversal work, while simpler median splits are faster to build. Dynamic scenes may refit boxes after deformation or rebuild the hierarchy when overlap grows. Correctness requires every primitive to remain enclosed; performance depends on tree quality and ray distribution.

Appendix.title: Camera calibration and bundle adjustment
Appendix.Content: Camera calibration and bundle adjustment
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Camera calibration estimates parameters that map 3D points to image coordinates. Intrinsics describe focal scale, principal point, and lens distortion; extrinsics describe camera pose relative to the scene. Known calibration targets provide 3D-to-2D correspondences, and a nonlinear least-squares objective minimizes reprojection error. Bundle adjustment jointly refines many camera poses and 3D feature points by minimizing all observed image residuals. The problem is sparse because each image sees only a subset of points. It also has gauge freedoms: translating or scaling the entire reconstruction may leave projections unchanged, so fix a reference pose or scale. Robust loss functions reduce the effect of mismatched features. Good initialization, parameter scaling, and Jacobian structure determine whether optimization converges.
Prerequisites
Used by
Full teaching explanation
Cameras, projection, and calibration · Pose estimation, transforms, and robust fitting · Stereo, relative orientation, and reconstruction
Phase 11 camera development

Linearize reprojection residuals as r(θ+δ)≈r(θ)+Jδ; the weighted information matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>J</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mi>W</mi> <mi>J</mi> </math> reveals parameter combinations that change observations. Null directions are local ambiguities, while small eigenvalues indicate weak constraints. In calibrated monocular structure from motion, global frame choice and common scene scale are gauge freedoms. Fix a pose and scale convention, or add a metric measurement, before interpreting covariance. Repeated nearly identical views may leave focal length, depth, and pose coupled even with many pixels. Appendix.title: Camera view and clip-space pipeline
Appendix.Content: Camera view and clip-space pipeline
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase7 · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A camera pose maps camera coordinates to world coordinates; its inverse is the view map. Projection produces homogeneous clip coordinates, clipping applies the API-specific inequalities, and valid perspective division produces NDC. Storage order supplies none of these coordinate contracts.
Reconstruction cue: A standard minus-Z perspective example needs a point in front of the camera and a meaningful clip w before division.
Prerequisites

Screen-space ray generation and mouse picking
Ray differentials and camera sampling measures

Appendix.Content: Recall and next depth
Reconstruct the example, state its conventions and find an input that violates its preconditions. Deeper algorithms and measured production performance remain separate from the present model.
Source and navigation
Continuous explanation · Coverage and source gap · Sources and verification
University course development

Extend the existing transform pipeline with the clipping and depth-precision decisions that make projection robust. A view frustum is the set of points a camera can see, bounded by near and far planes as well as image sides. Transforming the frustum into a canonical clip cube makes outside tests cheap; partially intersecting triangles must be clipped and triangulated so the rasterizer still receives triangles. The near plane also avoids geometry crossing the eye plane, while the far plane limits depth range. Floating-point depth values are unevenly distributed after perspective division, so an excessively tiny near distance paired with a huge far distance can make two nearby surfaces quantize to the same depth and produce z-fighting. Choose the narrowest useful depth interval and keep the view, clip, normalized, and screen coordinates distinct.
A scene description becomes an image · Cameras, projection, and calibration · Rasterization, coverage, and depth
Phase 11 camera development

A raster-to-ray camera maps a pixel to a geometric sample; In a pinhole model, invert projection and view transforms to recover a camera-space direction, then transform it to world space without applying translation as if it were a point. Pixel-center convention, viewport origin, handedness, clip-depth range, and normalization all affect the result. Offset a pixel to generate differential rays and estimate the surface footprint; that footprint grows with depth and changes with surface orientation. Keep ray generation distinct from raster projection while ensuring their conventions agree. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.

Appendix.title: Captured-world similarity alignment
Appendix.Content: Captured-world similarity alignment

Two reconstructions of the same scene can disagree by a similarity transform even when both are internally consistent. A similarity transform Sim(3) contains rotation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>R</mi> </math>, translation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>t</mi> </math> and a uniform scale <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>s</mi> </math>:
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>B</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mi>R</mi> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>A</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Rigid SE(3) alignment is the special case <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>s</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>.

This distinction matters when combining monocular/COLMAP-style reconstruction, device tracking, LiDAR geometry, Gaussian scenes or engine coordinates. A translation/rotation-only fit can look approximately correct near the alignment origin while scale error grows with distance.
Covariance transformation

A covariance represents second-order spread around the transformed mean. Translation does not affect covariance. Under the linear part <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>s</mi> <mi>R</mi> </math>,
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi> <mi>B</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mi>R</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi> <mi>A</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mi>R</mi> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>s</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi>R</mi> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi> <mi>A</mi> </msub> <msup> <mi>R</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: That <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>s</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </math> factor is required because variance has squared units.
Estimation

With corresponding point sets, similarity alignment can be estimated by centering the data, solving for rotation from cross-covariance, recovering scale from the centered energies, then translation from the transformed centroids. Robust systems must additionally handle outliers, degenerate configurations and coordinate-convention mistakes.

A good alignment report should include more than one mean error. Inspect residual distributions, spatial pattern, held-out correspondences and downstream image/depth consequences. A low training-set residual does not prove the transform generalizes.
Engine boundary

The alignment should be represented as one explicit typed transform with declared source and destination frames. Applying scale separately to positions while forgetting camera translations, covariance, velocity or distance thresholds creates a mixed-coordinate system.
Related: Gaussian covariance projection and footprint, Coordinate frames and change of basis, Conditioning and singularity.

Appendix.title: Clustered lighting depth slicing
Appendix.Content: Clustered lighting depth slicing

Clustered lighting partitions the camera frustum into three-dimensional cells and assigns lights to the cells they can influence. A fragment then tests only the lights attached to its cell rather than every light in the scene.

The screen dimensions are naturally tiled in x and y. Depth needs more care because perspective scenes can span orders of magnitude. Uniform linear z slices often waste many clusters far from the camera or give poor resolution near it.

A common logarithmic mapping for positive camera-space depth <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>z</mi> </math> between near <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>n</mi> </math> and far <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>f</mi> </math> is
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>t</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>log</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>log</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>f</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: then
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>s</mi> <mi>l</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>c</mi> <mi>e</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="INNER"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OPEN">⌊</mo> <mi>t</mi> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>z</mi> </msub> <mo data-mjx-texclass="CLOSE">⌋</mo> </mrow> <mo>,</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: clamped to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>z</mi> </msub> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math>.

Equal multiplicative depth ratios occupy equal widths in log space. With <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>n</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0.1</mn> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>f</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1000</mn> </math>, the decades 1→10 and 10→100 span the same number of ideal log slices.
Light assignment

Depth slicing alone does not make a clustered renderer. For each point/spot light, determine a conservative cluster range from its influence volume. Then append the light ID to every overlapping cluster.
The GPU implementation usually has two allocation problems:

ListItem.Content: count how many light references each cluster needs;
prefix-scan those counts to obtain compact non-overlapping list offsets;
fill the light-index array.

Appendix.Content: Atomic append alternatives exist, but they require overflow policy and contention measurement.
False positives versus false negatives

A conservative cluster test may include a light that ultimately contributes nothing to a fragment. That costs shading work but preserves correctness. A false negative drops illumination and is a correctness bug.
Cluster bounds therefore need to match the exact camera projection/depth convention, including reversed-Z if hardware depth is used to derive z.
Executable reference

tools/labs/realtime_rendering_reference_lab.cpp validates the logarithmic slice mapping, near/far clamping, monotonicity and equal-decade behavior. It does not yet implement full 3D light-volume/cluster intersection or GPU compaction.
Related: Prefix scan and stream compaction, Reversed-Z depth contracts.

Appendix.title: Collision barriers and continuous detection
Appendix.Content: Collision barriers and continuous detection
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A collision barrier turns a geometric safety condition into an optimization energy that rises sharply as bodies approach contact. Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) combines barrier terms for vertex-face and edge-edge separations with a time-step formulation that prevents interpenetration while a deformable object moves. Continuous collision detection (CCD) asks whether two moving primitives touch at any time during a step, not only at its endpoints; a pair can cross and separate between discrete samples. Robust CCD therefore needs conservative root bounds and careful handling of near-degenerate geometry. The barrier does not replace a correct collision set: missing pairs, invalid orientations, or a nonconservative CCD test can still allow tunneling. Very stiff barriers also make optimization ill-conditioned and require line search or step restrictions. IPC’s guarantees depend on assumptions about the initial configuration, collision constraints, and numerical tolerances. The core distinction is discrete overlap testing versus continuous-in-time contact prevention.

Appendix.title: Color encoding and linear-light operations
Appendix.Content: Color encoding and linear-light operations
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Color primaries/white point and nonlinear transfer encoding are different. Physical intensity filtering uses the appropriate linear quantity; black/white averaging then sRGB encoding gives about 0.735, not encoded 0.5. Tone/gamut mapping and absolute display luminance need separate contracts.
Prerequisites

Interpretation contract — A numeric sample requires a domain, units and encoding convention.

Source and navigation
Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map
University course development

Extend the existing color note with why image-processing arithmetic must distinguish encoded values from light. A display encoding such as sRGB uses a nonlinear transfer curve so code values allocate precision in a way that suits perception and storage. Averaging or adding those encoded numbers does not generally average or add emitted light. Decode to linear-light RGB before blending, filtering, estimating radiance, or compositing, then encode for display. If two equal-area samples contain linear intensities <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>0</mn> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> </math>, their physical average is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>0.5</mn> </math>; averaging their encoded sRGB values and treating that result as light yields a different, brighter answer. Color primaries and a white point also define the coordinate system of RGB, so a numeric triplet is incomplete without its color space. Keep scene-referred radiance, display-referred color, and perceptual appearance separate.
Color perception, encoding, and display · Light measurement and radiometry · Image sampling, filtering, and efficient reconstruction

Appendix.title: Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics
Appendix.Content: Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

Optimization chooses parameters to minimize an objective while satisfying constraints. Gradient descent steps opposite the gradient; Newton’s method also uses curvature, while quasi-Newton methods estimate curvature from gradient changes. Constraints may be enforced by parameterization, penalty terms, projection, or constrained solvers. In inverse kinematics, the parameters are joint angles and the objective measures distance between an end effector and its target. Forward kinematics maps angles to a hand or foot position; its Jacobian maps small joint changes to small endpoint changes. A damped least-squares step solves a stabilized linear system to reduce target error without exploding near singular poses. Joint limits, collisions, and multiple valid solutions make initialization and constraints important. The same framework applies to fitting cameras, deforming meshes, or matching image observations.
Phase 9–10 development

An optimization problem specifies an objective, variables, and equality or inequality constraints before an algorithm is selected. A gradient step uses first-order information; Newton and quasi-Newton steps add curvature, while line searches or trust regions control how far a local model is trusted. For nonlinear least squares, Gauss-Newton approximates curvature from the residual Jacobian and Levenberg-Marquardt damps the resulting system. Lagrange multipliers and KKT conditions describe constrained stationary points under their regularity assumptions. These local conditions do not by themselves prove global optimality.

Appendix.title: Contrastive vision and image-language alignment
Appendix.Content: Contrastive vision and image-language alignment
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Contrastive image-language learning trains an image encoder and a text encoder to place matching descriptions near their images in a shared feature space. For a batch of paired examples, cosine similarities between normalized embeddings form a score matrix; a temperature scales the scores, and an InfoNCE-style cross-entropy treats the matching pair as the positive while other batch items act as negatives. The objective makes retrieval and zero-shot label comparison possible by encoding class names as text. It learns statistical alignment, not a guarantee that every phrase is grounded in the pixels. Batch composition, duplicate or semantically similar negatives, captions, and web-data biases all shape the representation. A model may associate a prompt with correlated context rather than the requested object, and similarity scores are not calibrated probabilities. Evaluation must distinguish retrieval, classification, localization, and reasoning rather than treating one score as general visual understanding.

Appendix.title: Edge localization and subpixel contours
Appendix.Content: Edge localization and subpixel contours
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

An edge is a rapid image-intensity change, often associated with a material or depth boundary. Differentiating a noisy image amplifies high-frequency noise, so edge detectors first smooth with a Gaussian-like filter and then compute a gradient. Gradient magnitude estimates edge strength; gradient direction estimates the local normal. Nonmaximum suppression keeps a candidate only if it is a local maximum along that normal, thinning a broad response to a contour. Thresholding and hysteresis connect strong responses through weaker neighboring pixels. Subpixel localization fits a local peak to gradient samples, estimating a contour position between pixel centers. Accuracy depends on sampling, blur, contrast, and the assumed edge profile. This makes edge detection a measurement problem whose output uncertainty should propagate into later line, pose, or shape fitting.

Appendix.title: Exceptional projections and dimension
Appendix.Content: Exceptional projections and dimension
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Projection usually lowers dimension, but a finite or fractal set may collapse unusually many points in special directions. For a finite planar set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>X</mi> </math>, count pairs whose orthogonal projections coincide in direction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>θ</mi> </math>; such pairs lie on lines parallel to the projection fibers. Averaging over directions gives a baseline, while exceptional directions produce larger fibers and encode geometric structure. For a density, the related transform integrates along each fiber, as in tomography; the Fourier-slice identity connects the transform of a projection to a slice of the original Fourier transform. Dimension and separation assumptions matter: finite point sets, thickened sets, measures, and finite-field analogues have different statements. A highly structured set can defeat naive random-grid intuition, and subfield examples in finite fields create strong obstructions. Results are estimates with hypotheses, not universal formulas for every dimension or projection family. This node connects geometric projection to incidence counting and harmonic analysis.

Appendix.title: Fourier analysis and spectral phase
Appendix.Content: Fourier analysis and spectral phase
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Fourier coordinates encode frequency magnitude and phase; phase places structure. DFT analyzes a finite periodic block, FFT computes that transform efficiently, and finite-window leakage differs from bin spacing. Interior one-sided amplitude bins need conjugate-pair normalization.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Continuous signals and discrete samples — Filtering/frequency analysis operates on a declared domain and its samples.

Appendix.Content: Used by

ListItem.Content: Exceptional projections and dimension ## Recall and next depth

Appendix.Content: Recover the two tested sinusoid amplitudes and explain leakage. Pending: FFT implementations, windows and finite-boundary estimates. Written coverage is not a claim of learner mastery or accepted numbered-curriculum progress.
Source and navigation
Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map
University course development

Extend the existing frequency-domain treatment with visual interpretation and filtering consequences. A Fourier coefficient records how strongly a sinusoidal basis function occurs at a given frequency and phase. In images, the origin of a two-dimensional spectrum represents slow spatial variation; moving farther from it corresponds to finer variation. A broad bright center indicates low-frequency structure, while energy far from the center often represents edges and texture. Filtering multiplies each frequency by the filter response: a low-pass response suppresses fine detail, and a high-pass response emphasizes it. Aliasing folds unresolved high frequencies into lower ones because sampled sinusoids can share identical sample values. This explains moiré patterns and animated shimmer, and shows why a spectrum is useful for diagnosing sampling problems rather than only for theoretical signal processing.
Sampling continuous signals and image formation · Image sampling, filtering, and efficient reconstruction · Edges, contours, and subpixel localization

Appendix.title: GPU vertex specification
Appendix.Content: GPU vertex specification
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A GPU vertex-input specification explains how bytes in one or more buffers become per-vertex shader inputs. A buffer object owns bytes; a vertex array object records their interpretation: enabled attributes, component count and type, normalization, stride, byte offset, and the buffer binding used for fetch. Stride is the number of bytes between successive vertices; offset is the first component’s byte position. For vertex i, the address is base + offset + i × stride. For interleaved records containing position (3 floats), normal (3), and UV (2), the stride is 8 × 4 = 32 bytes and the UV offset is 24 bytes. Modern binding APIs separate attribute format from the buffer binding; older pointer-style calls can capture the buffer bound at setup time. A wrong stride may still address valid memory, so the symptom is often plausible but scrambled geometry. The contract must agree with CPU packing, shader input types, and the API’s state-capture rules.

Appendix.Content: Opacity accumulation is commutative under this formula, but color is generally not because earlier colors receive larger transmittance weights. Therefore sorting or another order-correct method is part of the image definition, not just an optimization.
Early termination

When <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>T</mi> </math> becomes small, later layers can contribute at most a small amount if color values are bounded. An early-out threshold is therefore an approximation with a measurable error bound. The threshold should not be mixed into the layer before deciding whether that layer contributes; candidate-transmittance and post-accumulation stopping can differ by one visible contributor.
Numerical stability

Large numbers of tiny alpha values can accumulate rounding error. Clamping alpha should follow a stated kernel/model rule rather than hide negative or greater-than-one values produced by an earlier bug.
Sorting precision also matters. If depth keys quantize several splats to the same value, the tie policy should be deterministic if reproducible images are required.

Appendix.title: Gaussian covariance projection and footprint
Appendix.Content: Gaussian covariance projection and footprint

A 3D Gaussian does not project to screen by simply projecting its center and keeping the same radius. Perspective is locally nonlinear, so the usual rasterization approximation linearizes the camera projection at the Gaussian center and propagates the 3D covariance through that local Jacobian.

Appendix.Content: Symmetry should also be preserved numerically up to rounding.
World covariance to camera covariance
If a Gaussian covariance is stored in world coordinates and the camera’s linear world-to-camera transform is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>R</mi> </math>, then
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>R</mi> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi> <mi>w</mi> </msub> <msup> <mi>R</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: For a rigid camera rotation, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>R</mi> </math> is orthogonal. For a similarity transform containing scale <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>s</mi> </math>, covariance scales by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>s</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </math> as well as rotating. Forgetting that square is a common alignment bug.

Many splat systems parameterize a positive covariance from scale and rotation rather than storing an arbitrary symmetric matrix. Whatever parameterization is used, the runtime should preserve positive-semidefinite structure instead of allowing an unconstrained matrix to become an invalid ellipse.
Ellipse footprint

A symmetric 2×2 projected covariance has eigenvalues <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo>≥</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>. The square roots are standard deviations along the principal screen-space axes. A conservative raster footprint can bound a chosen multiple of those standard deviations.
Adding a low-pass variance floor can stabilize subpixel Gaussians, but it changes the effective footprint. That is a quality/stability trade-off and should be measured, especially temporally.

Appendix.title: Hough transform and geometric voting
Appendix.Content: Hough transform and geometric voting
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

The Hough transform detects a parametric shape by letting each image feature vote for compatible shape parameters. A line can be represented by normal angle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>θ</mi> </math> and signed distance <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>ρ</mi> </math>, avoiding the vertical-line singularity of slope-intercept form. Each edge point votes along a curve in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>ρ</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>θ</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> space; a bin with many votes indicates a line supported by many image points. Circle detection adds center and radius parameters, increasing accumulator dimension and cost. Quantization controls a tradeoff: coarse bins merge nearby hypotheses but reduce precision; fine bins need more votes and memory. Gradient direction can restrict votes and reduce clutter. The transform tolerates missing edge segments because evidence accumulates globally, but unrelated edges can also create peaks, so candidates need geometric validation and robust fitting.

Appendix.title: Latent-variable models and generative flows
Appendix.Content: Latent-variable models and generative flows
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Generative models describe how data could be produced, often by first sampling a latent variable <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>z</mi> </math> and mapping it to an observation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> </math>. A variational autoencoder (VAE) learns an encoder distribution <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and decoder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mi>z</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>; its evidence lower bound balances reconstruction likelihood against a KL penalty that keeps the latent distribution tractable. A generative adversarial network (GAN) trains a generator against a discriminator, creating a game that can produce sharp samples but may be unstable or collapse to limited modes. Normalizing flows use invertible transformations so the data density can be computed with a change-of-variables Jacobian determinant. These methods solve different tradeoffs among likelihood, sample quality, latent structure, and optimization stability. Their assumptions matter: a VAE’s posterior family may be too simple, a GAN score is not a calibrated density, and a flow’s invertibility constrains architecture. Generated samples are not evidence that the model has learned the true causal process.

Appendix.title: Learned image features and CNNs
Appendix.Content: Learned image features and CNNs
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A convolutional neural network (CNN) learns filters that detect useful image patterns from data. A convolution layer applies the same small kernel at many image locations, so a feature such as an edge can be recognized wherever it appears. Early layers often respond to local contrast or texture; later layers combine these responses into task-specific patterns. Stride and pooling reduce spatial resolution, trading detail for computation and larger receptive fields. Training adjusts filter values by gradient descent using backpropagation and labeled or self-supervised objectives. Weight sharing gives translation equivariance: shifting an input shifts the feature map, but does not guarantee full translation invariance or robustness to scale, viewpoint, lighting, or distribution change. Padding and stride determine border behavior and output size; too much downsampling can erase small objects. A learned feature is a representation useful for a training objective, not a human-interpretable semantic guarantee. Performance depends on data coverage, augmentation, architecture, optimization, and honest held-out evaluation.

Appendix.title: Light spectra and radiometry
Appendix.Content: Light spectra and radiometry
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Light models distinguish wave propagation, photon energy and geometrical rays. Radiometry describes physical flux/radiance/irradiance; photometry adds standardized visual weighting. RGB requires an interpretation and cannot identify a unique spectrum.
Prerequisites
No formal graph prerequisite. Begin with the stated units and model; this is an independent-series foundation.

Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map
University course development

Radiometry distinguishes total radiant flux <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi> </math> in watts, irradiance <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>E</mi> </math> in watts per square metre, radiant intensity <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>I</mi> </math> in watts per steradian, and radiance <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>L</mi> </math> in watts per square metre per steradian measured with projected source area. A spectrum distributes the energy over wavelength; a three-channel RGB value is a measurement in a chosen color system and does not uniquely identify that spectrum. Solid angle measures directional extent rather than physical area. Consequently an area-light sample requires the projected-area and inverse-square Jacobian when expressed as a directional sample. Free-space radiance remains constant along an unobstructed ray, while irradiance from a point-like source changes with geometry. Photometry instead applies standardized visual weighting: luminous flux uses lumens, illuminance lux, and luminous intensity candela. These distinctions prevent treating brightness, exposure, flux and radiance as interchangeable scalar labels.

Appendix.title: Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure
Appendix.source: Concepts/Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure.md
Appendix.Content: Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A polygon mesh is a combinatorial surface made of vertices, edges, and faces plus an embedding that assigns each vertex a position. Manifoldness is a local connectivity condition: an interior edge belongs to two faces, and the faces around each interior vertex form one cycle or fan. At a boundary, an edge belongs to one face and the vertex neighborhood forms one open chain; each boundary component closes into a loop. A bow-tie vertex with two disconnected fans is nonmanifold even if every face is an ordinary triangle. These conditions let algorithms define an unambiguous local tangent neighborhood, traversal, and surface orientation. Connectivity validity does not guarantee good geometry: valid topology can still self-intersect, collapse to a point, or contain poor skinny triangles. Keep topological and geometric quality checks separate.

Appendix.title: Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance
Appendix.source: Concepts/Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance.md
Appendix.Content: Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Monte Carlo integration estimates an integral by averaging random samples with importance weights. For target integral <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>I</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∫</mo> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mi>x</mi> </math> and samples drawn from density <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, the estimator is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>I</mi> <mo stretchy="false">^</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>N</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <munderover> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>k</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. It is unbiased when samples cover every region where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>f</mi> </math> is nonzero and the density is correct. Its variance falls approximately as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </math>, so halving standard error takes about four times as many samples. Importance sampling chooses <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> </math> to follow the magnitude of the integrand; multiple importance sampling combines strategies such as light sampling and BSDF sampling with weights that avoid overtrusting a strategy that rarely finds a contribution. Path tracing applies these estimators to light paths, while rare caustics and narrow visibility openings remain high-variance cases.
Phase 9–10 development

For independent samples from density <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> </math>, the sample average estimates the integral using terms <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> </math> is positive on the integrand support. Unbiasedness requires the support condition and integrability; finite variance additionally requires a finite second moment of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>f</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </math>. A variance estimate describes sampling spread, not systematic bias. Dependent samples add covariance terms, and multiple-importance weights combine proposal densities while preserving mixture support. A confidence interval is justified only when its sampling and moment assumptions are stated.
Prerequisites

Appendix.title: ODE integration and stability
Appendix.Content: ODE integration and stability
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

An ordinary differential equation gives the rate of change of a state over time. Forward Euler uses the current derivative: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>k</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>t</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>h</mi> </math> is the time step. For decay <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>u</mi> <mo>˙</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mo>=</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mi>u</mi> </math>, it multiplies each step by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mo>−</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mi>h</mi> </math>; if the magnitude exceeds one, the numerical solution grows even though the true solution decays. Spring systems can be stiff because high-frequency modes force very small stable steps. Backward Euler evaluates the rate at the unknown new state and is more stable for decay but requires solving an equation and may add numerical damping. Symplectic Euler updates velocity then position and often keeps energy bounded for conservative mechanics. Choose an integrator according to stability, accuracy, conservation, and runtime rather than displayed frame rate alone.
Phase 9–10 development

An initial-value problem consists of a differential equation and a specified starting state. A numerical integrator replaces continuous evolution with finite updates, so accuracy and stability depend on both method and step size. Consistency concerns local approximation, stability concerns error growth under repeated steps, and convergence concerns the limiting solution as the step is refined. Stiff systems can force explicit methods to take very small steps even when the visible trajectory changes slowly. Symplectic methods preserve Hamiltonian structure but do not generally preserve exact energy at each step.
Prerequisites

Appendix.title: Optical flow and time to contact
Appendix.source: Concepts/Optical flow and time to contact.md
Appendix.Content: Optical flow and time to contact
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Optical flow is the apparent 2D motion of image features between frames. Under brightness constancy, a tracked point keeps approximately the same intensity as it moves, yielding the constraint <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi>x</mi> </msub> <mi>u</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi>y</mi> </msub> <mi>v</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>, where spatial derivatives <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi>x</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi>y</mi> </msub> </math> and temporal derivative <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </math> are measured from the image and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>v</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> is image velocity. One equation cannot determine two unknown components at a single pixel, so algorithms add neighborhood smoothness, feature tracking, or multiple scales. Flow can reveal camera motion, object motion, and looming. For an object approaching at speed <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>V</mi> </math>, its image size grows at a rate related to depth; the ratio of size to its time derivative estimates time to contact without separately knowing absolute scale under simplifying assumptions. Texture, occlusion, and illumination changes violate brightness constancy.

Appendix.title: PDE fields and discrete Laplacians
Appendix.Content: PDE fields and discrete Laplacians
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A partial differential equation constrains a field through spatial and temporal derivatives. Laplace’s equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math> seeks a harmonic field whose value matches its neighborhood average; Poisson’s equation adds a source term. On a regular grid, finite differences produce the five-point stencil with four neighbor weights and a negative center weight. On a triangle mesh, cotangent weights encode angles and a mass matrix normalizes by vertex area. Boundary conditions supply essential data: Dirichlet fixes values, Neumann fixes normal flux, and Robin combines them. Neumann Laplace systems require zero net flux and a pinned value or mean because constants lie in the nullspace. Explicit heat updates have a stability-limited time step; implicit updates solve a sparse system. PDE algorithms separate field representation, spatial operator, boundary conditions, and time integration.
Prerequisites

A valid finite-element cotangent stiffness can have negative edge weights while retaining nonnegative quadratic energy. Energy contraction, conservation and positivity of the evolving samples are separate requirements. The single-triangle derivation shows the distinction; the heat-step trace gives a negative sample while energy decreases.

Appendix.title: Perception feedback and robot learning
Appendix.Content: Perception feedback and robot learning
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A robot learning system closes a loop: sensors produce observations, a policy chooses an action, the world changes, and new observations arrive. A policy maps states or observations to actions; a value function estimates expected future return and can help compare actions. Reinforcement learning updates behavior from outcomes, while imitation learning fits demonstrations. In visual robotics, the observation pipeline may include cameras, learned features, pose estimates, and spatial grounding; errors then affect movement rather than only a label. The training and deployment distributions can differ because the robot’s own actions change what it sees. Small perception errors can compound into different states and larger future errors, a form of covariate or distribution shift. Stable deployment therefore needs calibrated sensing, feedback timing, safety constraints, and evaluation on physical conditions. Demonstrations in simulation do not establish robust real-world manipulation; embodiment, contact, latency, and unmodeled dynamics matter. A successful policy is evidence for a task and setting, not general intelligence.

Appendix.title: Quadric error mesh simplification
Appendix.Content: Quadric error mesh simplification
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Quadric error simplification greedily collapses the edge with the least predicted geometric error. For each triangle plane with unit normal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>n</mi> </math> and offset <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>d</mi> </math>, form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>v</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>x</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>y</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>z</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mi>d</mi> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi>T</mi> </msup> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>K</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>v</mi> <msup> <mi>v</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> </math>. A homogeneous point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>U</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi>T</mi> </msup> </math> has squared point-to-plane error <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>U</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mi>K</mi> <mi>U</mi> </math>. Sum the matrices of incident planes at each vertex; an edge candidate combines endpoint matrices. Partitioning the combined quadratic gives <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>Q</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mi>A</mi> <mi>x</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>b</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>c</mi> </math>, whose stationary point solves <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mi>x</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mi>b</mi> </math>. If the system is singular or indefinite, test endpoints and midpoint and keep the least-cost candidate. After selecting a location, reject collapses that flip incident face normals. The metric is a local approximation, so topology preconditions and orientation checks remain necessary.

Appendix.title: Quantization and compressed weights
Appendix.Content: Quantization and compressed weights
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C006
Definition and mechanism
Low-precision values and packed model weights reuse field-width, mask, shift, and bandwidth trade-offs.

Quantization maps a larger numeric domain to a smaller discrete set, usually with information loss. Packing stores those discrete codes compactly; dequantization reconstructs approximations. Bit packing alone is lossless for valid codes, whereas quantization changes represented precision.

M006 develops affine scales and zero points, local group calibration, offset-coded INT4, one-bit row centroids, metadata overhead and error metrics. Packing preserves discrete codes; quantization deliberately loses information. See the worked five-value group in the continuous story.

Appendix.title: Radiance fields and Gaussian splatting
Appendix.Content: Radiance fields and Gaussian splatting
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A radiance field represents a scene by the color and density seen along each 3D viewing ray. NeRF maps a position and viewing direction through a learned function, then volume-renders samples using transmittance and opacity weights; multiple calibrated photographs supervise the result. This representation handles view-dependent appearance but can require many ray samples and careful camera alignment. 3D Gaussian splatting instead stores anisotropic colored Gaussian primitives in space and projects them to screen, sorting and blending their footprints for fast interactive views. 2D Gaussian splatting uses oriented surface-like splats to improve geometric consistency. These methods trade continuous function evaluation for explicit primitives and rasterization. Sparse or biased views leave unseen regions unconstrained; floaters, blur, aliasing, incorrect transparency ordering, or poor geometry can remain even when training views look convincing. Novel-view quality is not equivalent to a watertight mesh or physically correct material. Reconstruction quality depends on camera poses, coverage, calibration, and the scene’s changing illumination.

Appendix.title: Ray-triangle intersection
Appendix.Content: Ray-triangle intersection
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A ray is a parametric half-line <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>r</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>o</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mi>d</mi> </math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>o</mi> </math> is its origin, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>d</mi> </math> is its direction, and only <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>t</mi> <mo>≥</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math> lies ahead of the ray. To intersect a triangle, first intersect the ray with its plane, then express the hit point in barycentric coordinates and accept it only if the weights lie inside the triangle. An equivalent determinant test solves for ray distance and two barycentric coordinates together. The hit record should state whether the result is nearest, any, or all intersections; those are different query contracts. Parallel or nearly parallel rays, degenerate triangles, and hits near edges require care because small floating-point errors can change classification. Scale-aware tolerances and consistent orientation predicates reduce cracks and self-intersection artifacts.

Extend the existing light-transport note with the distinction between a material’s directional response and the incident illumination it receives. At surface point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> </math>, outgoing radiance depends on emitted radiance plus an integral over incoming directions. The BRDF <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>r</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> is reflected outgoing radiance per incident irradiance, with units of inverse steradians; it depends on incoming direction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math> and viewing direction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> </math>. A physically plausible BRDF is nonnegative and conserves energy, but can still have narrow glossy lobes that are difficult to sample. The rendering equation combines this local material response with visibility, incoming radiance, and the cosine foreshortening factor. This form explains why shading, direct lighting, global illumination, and Monte Carlo integration are connected parts of one transport calculation rather than independent image effects.
Reflectance, BRDFs, and shading · The rendering equation and light transport · Numerical integration and Monte Carlo estimation

Appendix.title: Rendering history validity
Appendix.Content: Rendering history validity

A temporal renderer reuses information from earlier frames only if that information still estimates the same target quantity at the reprojected location. “Previous frame exists” is therefore not enough. History needs a validity contract.
A history sample may become invalid because of:

ListItem.Content: camera cuts or projection changes;
resize or dynamic-resolution changes;
object transform discontinuities;
newly visible or disoccluded surfaces;
material or lighting changes;
estimator changes such as sample pattern, exposure domain or denoiser configuration;
resource reallocation or version replacement.

Appendix.Content: Reprojection is a hypothesis

Motion vectors or previous transforms propose a correspondence from current sample to previous sample. The renderer should test that hypothesis with available evidence such as depth, normal, object/material identity, velocity magnitude or neighborhood statistics.
A common failure is using a valid coordinate that points to the wrong surface. Bounds checking prevents memory errors, not temporal ghosting.
Versioned history

Treat history like a cache with a key. Relevant state changes advance a version or invalidate specific history resources. The render graph can then express that a temporal pass consumes history version N and produces version N+1.

This is also important for progressive path tracing. Accumulation belongs to a camera/scene/material/light/estimator state. If any target-defining state changes and old samples remain, the output converges to a mixture of different images.
Failure-oriented tests

Useful temporal tests include a hard camera cut, a moving foreground object revealing background, an emissive material changing abruptly, resize, FOV change, jitter-sequence restart, and an object whose ID remains but geometry changes. For each case, record which history samples should survive and why.

The existing render-graph witness proves logical resource dependencies, not temporal validity itself. Native renderer evidence should capture motion/depth/ID buffers and show the acceptance/rejection mask.
Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Game Engine - From First Frame to Living Worlds#Let a renderer evolve without losing resource ownership.
Related: Temporal reprojection and history validation, Reversed-Z depth contracts.

Appendix.title: Sampling aliasing and reconstruction
Appendix.Content: Sampling aliasing and reconstruction
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Uniform samples identify frequencies only modulo sample rate and corresponding real-signal equivalences. Strictly band-limited ideal reconstruction needs non-overlapping spectral replicas; exact-Nyquist phase is a boundary hazard. Prefilter before decimation.
Phase 9–10 development

Signal aliasing occurs when distinct signal frequencies produce the same sampled values; reconstruction then cannot recover which signal generated the samples without additional assumptions. Stratification, low-discrepancy sequences, and blue-noise point sets describe where samples are placed, not a guarantee that the signal is band-limited or that an estimator is unbiased. Each strategy still needs a valid support, probability weight, and reconstruction filter.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Fourier analysis and spectral phase — Frequency and phase reveal transfer, sampling ambiguity and structural loss.

Appendix.Content: Used by

Content.Link: Sampling quality: stratification, quasi-Monte Carlo, and blue noise

ListItem.Content: Tensor-product interpolation ## Recall and next depth

Appendix.Content: Prove 13Hz and 3Hz sample identity at 10Hz. Pending: anisotropic/nonuniform sampling and actual reconstruction errors. Written coverage is not a claim of learner mastery or accepted numbered-curriculum progress.
Source and navigation
Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map
University course development

Sampling records measurements of a continuous signal on a discrete grid. Frequencies that differ by integer multiples of the sampling rate can produce the same samples, so the sampled values alone cannot identify which original signal was present. For ideal band-limited reconstruction, the signal must be restricted below half the sampling rate; equality at the limiting frequency needs additional phase and endpoint conditions. A real pixel also integrates light over area and exposure time, making its measurement a filtered sample. Prefiltering attenuates frequencies that would alias, while reconstruction estimates a continuous signal from the stored samples. Ideal sinc reconstruction has infinite support; practical filters trade computation, sharpness, ringing and residual aliasing. More samples reduce integration error only when their placement and weights match the intended pixel or path-space measure.
Sampling continuous signals and image formation · Image sampling, filtering, and efficient reconstruction

Appendix.title: Shadow filtering PCF and variance bounds
Appendix.source: Concepts/Shadow filtering PCF and variance bounds.md
Appendix.Content: Shadow filtering: PCF and variance bounds
A shadow map stores visibility information from a light-space camera. At shading time the receiver is projected into shadow-map coordinates and compared against stored depth.
The raw binary comparison is discontinuous. Filtering changes the estimator, and different methods filter different mathematical quantities.
Percentage-closer filtering
PCF performs several depth comparisons and averages the binary visibility results:

Appendix.Content: where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>b</mi> </math> is a declared bias under the shadow-map depth convention.
Filtering depths first and comparing once is not equivalent to averaging comparisons.
Bias is not a free visual knob. Constant/slope/normal-offset policies trade acne against detached shadows. The correct sign also depends on depth convention.
Variance shadow maps
VSM stores moments such as

Appendix.Content: Variance is

Appendix.Content: The moment representation can be filtered efficiently, but the probabilistic bound can cause light bleeding. Minimum variance clamps and light-bleeding reduction modify behavior and should be treated as approximations.

tools/labs/realtime_rendering_reference_lab.cpp computes a 3×3 PCF fraction on a hand-checkable map and checks that the VSM upper bound stays in [0,1] and decreases as a receiver moves farther beyond the mean blocker depth.
This does not prove cascade selection, perspective aliasing control, receiver-plane bias, EVSM, GPU sampling state or production shadow quality.

Appendix.title: Subdivision surface masks
Appendix.Content: Subdivision surface masks
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Subdivision refines a control mesh and updates old and newly inserted vertices with local masks, producing a sequence that approaches a smooth limit surface. Loop subdivision targets triangle meshes: for an interior edge with endpoints <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>b</mi> </math> and opposite vertices <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>c</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>d</mi> </math>, its new point is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>3</mn> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>8</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>c</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>8</mn> </math>. An old vertex of degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>n</mi> </math> becomes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>−</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mi>β</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>β</mi> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <msub> <mi>P</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math>, with the lecture’s simple weight <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>β</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>16</mn> </math> for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>n</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>3</mn> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>3</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>8</mn> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> otherwise. Catmull–Clark targets polygon meshes: face points are face-vertex averages, interior edge points average endpoints and two adjacent face points, and old vertices use face-average, edge-midpoint-average, and original-position terms. Boundary rules differ from interior masks and must be stated. Extraordinary vertices have nonregular valence and need deliberate treatment.

Appendix.title: Surface orientation from image brightness
Appendix.Content: Surface orientation from image brightness
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Shape-from-illumination methods infer surface orientation or depth from how light changes across an image. Photometric stereo observes a fixed camera view under multiple known light directions; for a Lambertian surface, measured intensity is proportional to albedo times the dot product between light direction and surface normal. Solving several such equations estimates the scaled normal, then integration recovers height up to boundary and scale ambiguities. A reflectance map plots brightness as a function of surface normal under fixed illumination and can reveal which orientations are visible. The extended Gaussian image maps each surface area to its normal on the unit sphere; its distribution summarizes orientation and convex shape properties. Shape-from-shading uses one image and must jointly reason about unknown lighting, albedo, and depth, so it is more ambiguous. Each method needs assumptions stated explicitly.

Appendix.title: Template matching and distance transforms
Appendix.Content: Template matching and distance transforms
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Template matching searches an image for a known pattern by comparing a small reference patch at candidate positions. Sum of squared differences penalizes intensity mismatch; normalized correlation compensates for brightness scale and offset. Direct search costs work proportional to image area times template area, while convolution or Fourier methods can accelerate broad searches. Rotation and scale changes require transforming the template or searching additional parameters. For contour-based matching, a distance transform stores each pixel’s distance to the nearest edge. A template edge point then receives a low cost when it lands near an observed contour even if the exact pixels do not align. The chamfer score sums these distances over template points. These methods suit industrial inspection where the target geometry is known, but need explicit thresholds for occlusion, deformation, and false positives.
Prerequisites
Used by
Full teaching explanation

Appendix.title: Temporal history validation and reprojection
Appendix.Content: Temporal history validation and reprojection

Temporal rendering reuses information from earlier frames, but the old sample is useful only when it still estimates the same current surface and the same target quantity. Reprojection therefore proposes a correspondence; validation decides whether to trust it.
Under one common screen-space convention, a motion vector stores
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>m</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>u</mi> <msub> <mi>v</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>p</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mi>e</mi> <mi>v</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mi>s</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>−</mo> <mi>u</mi> <msub> <mi>v</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>c</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mi>e</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: so the history lookup is
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>u</mi> <msub> <mi>v</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>h</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>s</mi> <mi>t</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mi>y</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>u</mi> <msub> <mi>v</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>c</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mi>e</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Other engines store the opposite sign. The important requirement is that the convention is stated once and tested by projecting the same point in current and previous camera transforms.
Validation signals
A history sample should be rejected when evidence says the reprojected location belongs to a different target. Useful signals include:

ListItem.Content: out-of-bounds previous UV;
camera-cut/history-generation mismatch;
depth disagreement;
normal disagreement;
object/material/primitive identity mismatch;
invalid velocity;
resize or projection change;
estimator/material/lighting changes that invalidate the accumulated quantity.

Appendix.Content: Depth thresholds should be scale-aware. A fixed absolute depth epsilon that works at one metre may be useless at one kilometre.
Disocclusion

Disocclusion is the classic temporal failure. A foreground object moves away and reveals background. The motion vector can point to a valid previous pixel, but that pixel represented the foreground. Bounds checks succeed while semantics fail. Depth/ID/normal validation is therefore about surface correspondence, not memory safety.
Accumulation and clamping

Once history is accepted, a temporal filter blends current and historical estimates. A high history weight reduces noise but increases lag and ghosting. Neighborhood clipping, variance clipping, reactive masks and confidence weighting are ways to constrain history when local evidence changes.
Those techniques should be tested on controlled sequences: static scene, camera pan, hard cut, moving foreground revealing background, emissive change, thin geometry and high-frequency texture.
Executable reference

tools/labs/realtime_rendering_reference_lab.cpp defines an explicit history predicate using bounds, history generation, object identity, relative depth and normal agreement. Tests cover a stable sample, camera cut, disocclusion, depth jump and off-screen reprojection. It also verifies the declared motion-vector sign and that invalid history contributes zero weight.
This is a CPU semantic oracle. It does not yet implement TAA neighborhood clipping, jitter, full screen reprojection or GPU parity.
Related: Rendering history validity, Reversed-Z depth contracts.

Appendix.title: Temporal reprojection and history validation
Appendix.Content: Temporal reprojection and history validation
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: XR01
Definition and mechanism

Reprojection aligns history with a current target; disocclusion exposes content with no matching old observation. Validated blending trades noise against response/ghosting. Gaze-driven quality changes also change history reliability; TAA is not exposure integration.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Spatiotemporal sampling and retinal motion — Temporal reuse must respect changing scene and retinal observations.
Antialiasing and sample allocation — History depends on the actual current/prior sampling strategy.

Source and navigation
Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map
Phase 11 camera development

Reprojection predicts where a prior sample lands under camera and object motion. Depth agreement tests whether the same visible surface likely occupies that location, but cannot prove stored color remains valid after lighting, exposure, material, or sampling changes. Combine projected position, depth tolerance, and disocclusion checks; reduce history weight when confidence is low. Monocular reconstruction has arbitrary global scale, so metric depth thresholds require an external scale or consistent units. Reprojection success is geometric evidence, not a photometric guarantee. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.
Neighborhood clipping and deterministic jitter witness
tools/labs/realtime_effects_reference_lab.cpp now extends history validity into two mechanisms that directly affect temporal stability.

The first is deterministic subpixel jitter generated from Halton bases 2 and 3. The sample lies inside one pixel but changes frame to frame, allowing temporal accumulation to observe different subpixel locations. A jitter sequence must be owned by the camera/projection history contract: if the current and previous transforms disagree about whether jitter is included, the motion vector and reprojection become inconsistent.

The second is neighborhood clipping. A reprojected history value can be geometrically valid yet photometrically stale after disocclusion or fast shading change. The smallest CPU oracle clamps the history sample into the current 3×3 neighborhood min/max interval before blending. Production TAA often uses variance-guided bounds, color-space transforms, reactive masks and velocity-dependent weighting, but the invariant remains: history should not inject values unsupported by the current local evidence.

The laboratory checks known first Halton points, uniqueness over an initial sequence, bright/dark history rejection and preservation of an in-range history value. It remains a semantic oracle rather than a complete production TAA implementation.

Appendix.title: Triangle rasterization and coverage tests
Appendix.Content: Triangle rasterization and coverage tests
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Rasterization converts triangle geometry into a finite set of image samples. A pixel’s ideal coverage is the area fraction inside the triangle; a center test approximates this integral with one binary answer and therefore creates jagged edges. A directed edge defines an inside half-plane, so three signed edge tests classify a point against a triangle. A consistent tie rule assigns samples exactly on shared edges to one triangle, preventing cracks and double coverage. Supersampling tests several locations per pixel and averages their coverage, trading cost for a better area estimate. Hardware often checks candidate samples in parallel within a bounding box, then rejects or accepts coarse blocks that are wholly outside or inside. Triangle coverage is also the basis for interpolating depth, color, normals, and texture coordinates.

Nearby pixels define nearby directions; their derivatives estimate how a finite pixel footprint expands on a surface. Visual angle measures directional separation, while ray differentials describe local change in generated rays and may include lens sampling. Scene → display light → optics → retina → task; gaze feeds rendering decisions.
Qualitative AI illustration; not calibrated rays or anatomical dimensions.
Vergence points the eyes; accommodation changes focus. A near stereo target can coexist with a distant optical image.
Demanded distances can disagree; sharpness alone cannot fix that.
At 10 Hz, 13 Hz and 3 Hz cosines give identical samples: their phase difference is whole cycles.
Filter before reducing sample rate; more bits cannot recover lost distinctions.
Black/white mean is 0.5 linear → about 0.73536 sRGB. Encoded mean 0.5 → about 0.21404 linear.
Values are normalized channels, not nits. Specify the encoding and arithmetic domain.
Predict gaze for visible time; expand the sharp region for measured uncertainty.
A 90 Hz stream gives 11.11 ms intervals, not a latency measurement.
