Appendix.Content: From emitted light to a perceptual claim

Caption: The rendering loop is closed: the display changes the light reaching the observer, and observer/task conditions shape what counts as visible. RGB code values are not spectra and are not automatically linear-light energy.
Four measurement families that must not be collapsed
Caption: A metric score is not a direct reading of human experience. Each transformation adds assumptions and conditions.

Cell.Content: Question
Distinction to retrieve
How much physical light?
Radiant power/energy and radiance/irradiance are different quantities.
What color signal?
Spectrum and colorimetric coordinates are not interchangeable.
What does the eye resolve?
Acuity varies with eccentricity, contrast, adaptation and task.
Is the displayed result equivalent?
Focus/accommodation and binocular vergence can conflict in stereoscopic displays.
Does a score prove improvement?
Only for the metric, conditions, observers and task actually tested.

Appendix.Content: Sampling and filtering: preserve what can be distinguished

Caption: Sampling without suitable filtering can make distinct signals produce identical samples. A pixel footprint, motion, and time interval all matter; one isolated pixel center is not a complete image measurement.
Temporal reuse is a correspondence hypothesis
Caption: Reprojection is not “old pixels are correct.” It is a prediction plus validation. Jitter, temporal antialiasing and motion blur address related but distinct problems.
Foveation is a budget under uncertainty

Appendix.Content: Caption: Less shading work does not imply the whole frame becomes equally faster. Prediction error, transition smoothness, display timing and workload determine the usable benefit.
Retrieval prompts

ListItem.Content: Why can two different continuous signals produce the same samples?
How do sampling rate, filter footprint and reconstruction relate?
What changes between linear-light averaging and averaging encoded RGB values?
Why can a sharp stereo image still feel uncomfortable?
What evidence is needed before a threshold can be treated as a boundary?
Why does valid foveation require a margin for gaze prediction error?

BlockQuote.Content: [!answer]- Compact key Frequencies beyond the sampling system’s distinguishable range can alias. Filtering limits content before discrete sampling; reconstruction defines what is inferred between samples. Nonlinear transfer encoding changes averages. Accommodation and vergence can demand different focal distances. A threshold depends on procedure and conditions, not just a fitted curve. Gaze latency/error can move the true fovea outside a region sized only around the estimate.

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Convex combinations and convex hulls — Convex combinations and convex hulls Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6 Definition and mechanism Affine point combinations have weights summing to one. Convex combinations additionally have nonnegative weights. A convex set contains every segment between its members; a convex hull is the smallest such set containing supplied points. The panel is the convex hull of its corners. A filled disk is convex; its boundary alone is not. Prerequisites
Barycentric coordinates and interpolation — Affine weights establish origin-independent combinations and inside-hull restrictions.

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Barycentric coordinates and interpolation — Barycentric coordinates and interpolation Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Barycentric weights reconstruct a triangle point as an affine combination. The weights sum to one; nonnegative weights describe points inside or on a nondegenerate triangle. Dot-system solves on off-plane inputs describe their projection, not proven surface membership. The panel sensor <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> has weights <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>5</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>12</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>3</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and corner temperatures <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>20</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>40</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>50</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> interpolate to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>35</mn> </math>. Prerequisites
Gram matrices and coordinate metrics — Pairwise basis measurements define the systems and metric used in reconstruction. Vectors coordinates and affine points — Point, displacement and coordinate roles determine which geometric operations are meaningful.
Used by
Convex combinations and convex hulls — Builds on this mechanism in the connected geometry story. Triangle rasterization and coverage tests Ray-triangle intersection Stereo correspondence and epipolar geometry Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation Interpolation versus approximation ## Recall and next depth
Derive signed-area ratios; distinguish affine attribute interpolation from perspective-correct screen interpolation. Full production proofs, target-specific integration and learner mastery require further evidence. Source and navigation Teaching narrative · Coverage and source gap · Evidence and limits · Dependency Map University course development Extend the existing interpolation note with the geometric meanings that make triangle rasterization and camera calibration easier to reason about. For triangle vertices <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </math>, a point inside can be written <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </math>, where the weights sum to one and are nonnegative. Each weight is the area of the opposite subtriangle divided by the full triangle area; equivalently it is a signed edge-distance normalized by altitude. The weights therefore provide both a point-in-triangle test and attribute interpolation. They also reveal a limitation: screen-space weights do not linearly interpolate a 3D attribute after perspective projection. Interpolate reciprocal depth and attribute divided by depth, then divide the interpolated values to recover perspective-correct texture coordinates or colors. Rasterization, coverage, and depth · Textures and surface detail · Pose estimation, transforms, and robust fitting. Open Barycentric coordinates and interpolation in Volume 2

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Off-axis stereo projection and disparity — Off-axis stereo projection and disparity Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11 Definition and mechanism Stereo cameras use two eye centres separated by a baseline, while each projection frustum is shifted so a chosen zero-parallax plane aligns in the images. Parallel eye orientations with asymmetric frusta avoid the vertical mismatch and discomfort often introduced by toe-in cameras. For rectified pinhole cameras, disparity is approximately <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi> <mi>x</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>x</mi> </msub> <mi>B</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>Z</mi> </math>, so inferred depth is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>Z</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>x</mi> </msub> <mi>B</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi> <mi>x</mi> </math> under the calibration and rectification assumptions. Depth uncertainty grows roughly with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>Z</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </math> for fixed pixel disparity error. Distinguish interpupillary distance from lens and display-centre spacing; the rendered baseline is an optical/comfort design decision. Use consistent pixel units for focal length, baseline, and disparity before computing metric depth. Prerequisites
Stereo correspondence and epipolar geometry Camera calibration and bundle adjustment Axial depth and Euclidean range

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Tensor-product interpolation — Tensor-product interpolation Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism Bilinear and trilinear interpolation apply one-dimensional linear weights independently along each coordinate axis. In a rectangular cell, each corner contributes the product of its axis weights; the weights are nonnegative and sum to one for coordinates inside the cell. This preserves the range of scalar corner values, but the interpolated surface can be twisted rather than planar, and derivatives may jump across cell boundaries. For a voxel field, trilinear interpolation provides a continuous in-cell estimate; differentiating it yields a local gradient, which need not have unit length even when samples approximate signed distance. Keep coordinates normalized to the cell and define behavior outside the sampled grid explicitly. Prerequisites
Interpolation versus approximation Sampling aliasing and reconstruction

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content: This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Sampling support and missing strata — Sampling support and missing strata The support of a sampling distribution is the set of outcomes it can generate with nonzero probability. Importance sampling can change how often regions are visited, but it cannot estimate a nonzero contribution from a region that the estimator never samples unless another technique covers that region. For an integral <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>I</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∫</mo> <mi>D</mi> </msub> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mi>d</mi> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> </math> an ordinary importance estimator using density <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>I</mi> <mo stretchy="false">^</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>N</mi> </mfrac> <munderover> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>∼</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo>.</mo> </math> This requires <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>></mo> <mn>0</mn> </math> wherever <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> contributes to the target integral, up to measure-zero exceptions. If a region has nonzero integral but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math> there, taking more samples from the existing support cannot repair the missing contribution. The estimator converges to the wrong target. Stratification Partition domain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>D</mi> </math> into strata <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>D</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> </math>. A correct stratified estimator accounts for each stratum’s measure/probability. If a 3×3 pixel partition has nine equal cells but the algorithm always samples only the first five and treats their mean as the full-pixel mean, it has changed the integration domain. Randomly selecting strata with the appropriate selection probability can remain unbiased; permanently omitting fixed strata cannot. MIS support Multiple importance sampling can repair a weak proposal when another technique covers the missing region and the combined estimator uses compatible PDFs. The PDFs must include discrete technique/light selection probabilities as well as continuous densities. Debugging Visualize sample positions and build a support occupancy histogram. Many “mysterious bias” bugs become obvious when entire regions are empty. For image-space algorithms, also test edges/corners of the reconstruction filter, not only the pixel center. Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#A missing region cannot be repaired by taking more samples there. Related: Multiple importance sampling, Latin-hypercube sampling, Antialiasing and sample allocation.. Open Sampling support and missing strata in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Camera gauge freedoms and observability — Camera gauge freedoms and observability Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 Definition and mechanism A gauge freedom is a coordinated change to unknown scene and camera parameters that leaves every measured image unchanged. In calibrated monocular structure from motion, translating and rotating the entire reconstruction changes only the chosen world frame, while a common scale change of points and camera translations preserves projections; absolute metric scale therefore needs an external reference. Observability asks which local parameter changes produce distinguishable measurements. Linearizing reprojection residuals gives a Jacobian; its weighted information tensor or matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>J</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mi>W</mi> <mi>J</mi> </math> reveals weak parameter combinations through small eigenvalues after gauge directions are fixed. Example: adding more points to one planar, nearly fronto-parallel view may reduce pixel noise while focal length and distance remain strongly coupled. These conclusions assume a stated camera/scene model, correctly associated observations, and local linearization; the information matrix diagnoses local constraints, not global uniqueness. Report uncertainty only after fixing the gauge and specifying the observation noise model. Example: A monocular map can be uniformly enlarged with all camera translations enlarged by the same factor and render the same images; a known baseline or measured object length fixes that scale gauge. Assumptions: The gauge statement assumes calibrated monocular perspective cameras and no metric prior.; The information-matrix interpretation is local and depends on residual weighting and parameterization. Prerequisites
Camera calibration and bundle adjustment Coordinate frames and change of basis Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Vector spaces subspaces and span — Vector spaces subspaces and span Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6 Definition and mechanism A vector space is closed under addition and field-scalar multiplication with coherent algebraic laws. A subspace retains these operations inside a larger space. The span of generators is every finite linear combination of them. The plane <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>z</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math> is a subspace of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi> </mrow> <mn>3</mn> </msup> </math>; <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>z</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math> is an affine translate, not a subspace. The span of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> contains all in-plane movements. Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Half-edge mesh connectivity — Half-edge mesh connectivity Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism A half-edge data structure stores each undirected edge as two opposite directed records. Each record points to its twin, the next directed edge around its face, its origin vertex, its edge, and its face; vertices, edges, and faces keep one representative half-edge. Repeatedly following next visits a face boundary. Following twin then next walks around a vertex fan. This makes local neighborhoods and edits proportional to local degree rather than requiring a scan of every face. Correctness depends on invariants: twin of twin returns to the original, a half-edge is not its own twin, and next pointers form closed face cycles. The representation naturally assumes manifold connectivity; it can encode flips, splits, and collapses by changing a bounded set of pointers, but careless updates can break the cycles and corrupt subsequent traversal. Prerequisites
Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Coordinate frames and change of basis — Coordinate frames and change of basis Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase7 · Latest development: Phase7 Definition and mechanism A frame gives an origin and independent axes relative to another frame. Its matrix maps local coordinates to that parent description. Changing description uses the inverse destination frame followed by the source frame; active motion and passive coordinate change answer different questions. Reconstruction cue: Coordinates from frame A to frame B use inverse(F_B) times F_A. Prerequisites
Linear affine and projective transformations Matrix inversion pivoting and residuals
Used by
Camera view and clip-space pipeline Transform hierarchies TRS and shear Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics Camera gauge freedoms and observability

Deeper algorithms and measured production performance remain separate from the present model. Source and navigation Continuous explanation · Coverage and source gap · Sources and verification Phase 11 camera development A basis change re-expresses the same physical points and transforms; a reconstruction gauge allows different parameter assignments to produce identical measurements. Fixing one camera pose chooses a world origin and orientation, but adds no image evidence. Monocular scale remains free until a baseline, known length, or metric sensor anchors it. Do not mistake a coordinate convention for an empirical measurement. This distinction matters when defining bundle-adjustment priors and covariance, and assumes a rigid calibrated camera model. Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Hardware depth-buffer linearization — Hardware depth-buffer linearization Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11 Definition and mechanism Perspective projection maps axial distance nonlinearly into NDC depth. For a declared projection depth row <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mi>A</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>B</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>d</mi> </math>, solve <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>d</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>B</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>q</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>A</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>; finite conventional, finite reversed, infinite reversed, and OpenGL-style conventions have different coefficients or NDC conversions. The depth sample must first be interpreted in the same range and direction used by the projection matrix. This is why a single generic formula without an API and projection contract is unsafe. Verify near and far endpoints, test round trips over a range of distances, and handle an infinite-far endpoint such as reversed depth <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math> explicitly. Near/far endpoint checks catch sign mistakes immediately; interior round trips then test scaling and finite precision. Prerequisites
Camera view and clip-space pipeline Axial depth and Euclidean range Depth buffering and visibility order

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Bit packing — Bit packing Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C001 Definition and mechanism Multiple constrained values share a carrier word; extraction and mutation must preserve the declared schema. Packing places several constrained values into a carrier. Input [1,0,1,1,0,1,0,1] packed LSB-first produces 0xAD. Unpacking needs the logical count because the final byte may contain unused bits. Define whether padding must be zero, ignored, or rejected. Prerequisites
Bit field — A field is a declared range with offset s and width w, not automatically a C++ language bit-field member. Bitwise OR — Per lane: only 0|0 is 0; the other three cases are 1. Interpretation contract — For 0xAD, unsigned interpretation gives 173; eight-bit two’s complement gives −83.

Quantization and compressed weights — uses bit packing as part of its representation or reasoning.

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content: This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Singular value decomposition — Singular value decomposition For any real rectangular matrix, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>U</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi> <msup> <mi>V</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </msup> </math>. Right singular vectors are input directions, left singular vectors are output directions, and nonnegative singular values are principal stretches. Unlike eigenvectors, the two sets live in different spaces. Use it when: revealing rank and conditioning, solving rank-uncertain least squares, compressing a matrix, or understanding PCA. Developed in Phase 8: The SVD expresses a rectangular map using orthonormal input and output directions joined by nonnegative stretches. Full, thin, and compact shapes have different dimensions; bidiagonal reduction and Jacobi methods compute the factors, and reconstruction, orthogonality, and triplet residuals check them independently. factor shapes · SVD algorithms and validation Prerequisites Matrix multiplication and composition order, Eigenvalues and eigenspaces, Dot products and orthogonality. Used by Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse, PCA and covariance eigensystems, Polar decomposition, Matrix factorization choices. Teaching path: SVD geometry. - Matrix norms and numerical error — Extends this foundation into the Phase 8 dependency spine. - Camera calibration and bundle adjustment - Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics University course development Extend the existing factorization note with its role in estimation, conditioning, and geometry. For matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> </math>, the decomposition <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>U</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi> <msup> <mi>V</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> </math> separates orthogonal input directions, axis-aligned scaling, and orthogonal output directions. Singular values on the diagonal of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi> </math> quantify how strongly each independent direction is preserved; a zero or tiny value signals rank loss or poor conditioning. Least-squares fitting can use this structure to identify which parameter combinations are well constrained and to avoid amplifying measurement noise along nearly invisible directions. The same analysis explains why a camera calibration or bundle-adjustment system can have gauge freedoms: translating or scaling the entire reconstruction may leave image measurements unchanged. Singular values diagnose these ambiguities, while constraints or fixed reference poses remove them. Thus SVD links linear algebra to robust vision, not just matrix compression. Pose estimation, transforms, and robust fitting · Stereo, relative orientation, and reconstruction · Optimization, constraints, and inverse kinematics. Open Singular value decomposition in Volume 2

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Lens optics and depth of field — Lens optics and depth of field Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism A pinhole camera maps every scene point to one image point through a single center, but a real lens has a finite aperture. Rays from one object point pass through different parts of the aperture and meet at a focused image point only for the chosen focus distance. Points nearer or farther from that plane form a blur disk called the circle of confusion. Stopping down the aperture narrows the cone of rays and increases depth of field, but reduces collected light and may require longer exposure or higher sensor gain. Focal length and focus distance also affect field of view and perspective magnification. A thin-lens model is an approximation; real lenses add aberrations and vignetting. The model helps explain why depth of field is both an optical effect and a sampling/integration process over aperture positions. Prerequisites
Camera view and clip-space pipeline Reflection refraction and shading directions
Used by
Worlds, Images and Inference Exposure and sensor response Ray differentials and camera sampling measures
Full teaching explanation Lens optics, focus, and image formation · Photographic composition, history, and communication · Photographic workflow and integrated decisions Phase 11 camera development A pinhole camera emits one ideal ray per image location. A finite-aperture lens samples a family of rays whose intersections form a blur disk away from the focal plane. A thin-lens camera therefore samples film and lens position, then aims through a focal point. Differentials from film offsets alone omit aperture variation unless the model includes it. Monte Carlo PDFs and camera weights must match the sampled film/aperture measure. The thin-lens model approximates real optics; aberrations and bokeh shape require richer models. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.. Open Lens optics and depth of field in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Reversed-Z depth contracts — Reversed-Z depth contracts A depth buffer stores an ordering coordinate, not Euclidean distance. Reversed-Z changes the mapping so near geometry receives larger depth values and far geometry approaches zero. The precision advantage comes from combining the reciprocal structure of perspective depth with floating-point numbers whose representable values are denser near zero. The entire renderer has to agree on the convention. Reversing only the projection matrix while keeping old clear/comparison assumptions creates a system that is internally contradictory. Contract checklist For a conventional zero-to-one API depth range, a common reversed-Z setup uses:
near plane mapped near 1; far distance mapped toward 0; depth buffer cleared to 0; comparison set to GREATER or GREATER_EQUAL; hierarchical depth/occlusion reductions defined consistently with “larger is nearer”; screen-space reconstruction derived from the exact projection convention.
Infinite-far reversed projection can remove an explicit far-plane distance from the perspective matrix, but frustum/culling policy still needs a practical world-space bound when the application cannot process infinite geometry. Why floating point helps Perspective depth is approximately affine in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>z</mi> </math>. Conventional mapping spends many floating-point representable values near depth one, where far geometry is crowded. Reversed-Z places far geometry near zero, where floating-point exponent scaling gives much more useful relative spacing. With integer/fixed-point depth, reversal alone does not create the same dramatic distribution advantage; the floating-point representation is part of the argument. Reconstruction must use the actual matrix Do not paste a “linearize depth” formula from another API. Different clip-space ranges, handedness, finite/infinite far planes and reversed mappings change the coefficients. A robust reconstruction derives camera-space position from the same projection matrix or stores explicit projection parameters and tests known near/far points. Occlusion and temporal systems Hierarchical Z, SSAO, SSR, clustered depth slicing, picking and temporal rejection all consume depth meaning. Every reduction or comparison must be audited when the convention changes. A min-reduction hierarchy written for standard depth may need a max-reduction interpretation under reversed-Z. Tests Project known camera-space depths, confirm monotonic ordering, quantize them to the real depth format, reconstruct them, and measure relative world-space error over logarithmically spaced distances. Also test clear-value behavior with an empty frame and a near geometry sample. Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#Give depth an explicit meaning. Related: Hardware depth-buffer linearization, Rendering history validity.. Open Reversed-Z depth contracts in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Nonlinear least squares: Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt — Nonlinear least squares: Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism Nonlinear least squares minimizes one half the squared norm of a residual vector. Its gradient and Hessian involve the residual Jacobian; the exact Hessian also contains second derivatives of each residual. Gauss–Newton drops those latter terms, producing a positive-semidefinite normal matrix and an efficient local step when residuals are small or the model is close to linear. Levenberg–Marquardt adds damping to control ill-conditioned or overly aggressive steps, blending Gauss–Newton with gradient descent. These algorithms are useful for camera calibration, bundle adjustment, and geometric fitting. Residual scaling, parameter units, rank deficiency, and gauge freedoms influence the solution. Normal equations can square the condition number, so QR or other structured solves may be safer. A small residual does not prove parameters are identifiable or physically correct. Prerequisites
Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks Hessians and local curvature Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics
Used by

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Position reconstruction from depth — Position reconstruction from depth Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11 Definition and mechanism Given a pixel and an axial depth value, reconstruct a view-space point by converting the pixel to NDC, forming its camera ray, and scaling that ray so its forward-axis component equals the measured depth. Alternatively, transform the corresponding homogeneous clip point through an inverse projection matrix and divide by its resulting homogeneous coordinate. To obtain world position, apply the inverse view transform. These routes must share the actual viewport, pixel-centre, NDC-depth, and projection conventions used to render the image. In large worlds, subtract camera-relative origins before reducing precision; converting an already-rounded coordinate cannot restore lost detail. In a camera-relative renderer, reconstruct near the camera origin before adding a large global offset. Prerequisites
Axial depth and Euclidean range Hardware depth-buffer linearization Camera calibration and bundle adjustment Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division
Used by

A policy states the intended response to an unrepresentable answer: wrap modulo a base, report checked failure, widen storage, clamp to an endpoint, or grow arbitrary precision. Choose by subsystem meaning. Color-byte output and hash arithmetic need different policies. Prerequisites

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Robust geometric predicates — Robust geometric predicates Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6 Definition and mechanism A geometric predicate decides a category from a sign, such as orientation. Near cancellation, ordinary floating arithmetic may not certify that sign. Adaptive arithmetic adds work only when justified error bounds leave uncertainty. Exact stored-input decisions cannot restore rounded-away physical information. A triangle can have an accurately small area estimate yet an uncertified orientation sign. Declaring every small value zero changes topology instead of proving a decision. Prerequisites
Cross products and oriented area — Oriented area supplies face normals, frame signs and geometric determinants. Dot and cross-product rounding — Cancellation and rounded inputs explain when a determinant sign or finite measurement is uncertain.
Used by Later curriculum sources can deepen this same node; no future coverage is marked complete.
Collision barriers and continuous detection ## Recall and next depth
Distinguish tolerance-based geometry, measurements and certified predicates; the Phase 6 lab implements only ordinary tests. Full production proofs, target-specific integration and learner mastery require further evidence. Source and navigation Teaching narrative · Coverage and source gap · Evidence and limits · Dependency Map Phase 11 camera development Adaptive orientation and incircle predicates protect discrete sign decisions from floating-point error by refining arithmetic when an error bound cannot certify the result. Camera estimation has a different uncertainty: noisy pixels and weak observability can leave pose uncertain even when every sign is exact. Predicate robustness does not improve measurement accuracy, and a low reprojection residual does not guarantee every combinatorial decision was reliable. Keep layers distinct: use robust predicates for topology, uncertainty weights for image residuals, and Jacobian spectra for weak directions. Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation — Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism After a vertex is transformed, its clip-space coordinate is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>z</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Clip primitives against the view volume before perspective division; under the conventional OpenGL clip convention the inequalities are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>≤</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>z</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>≤</mo> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> </math>. A crossing edge is split by interpolating its homogeneous endpoints, which preserves the projective line and avoids dividing by a small or negative <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>w</mi> </math> too early. Only surviving points are divided by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> </math> to enter normalized device coordinates. Attributes then need perspective-correct interpolation: screen-space barycentric weights interpolate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>w</mi> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>w</mi> </math>, and the fragment value is their ratio. For a triangle with weights <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Direct linear interpolation in screen space is correct only for affine quantities or equal depth; otherwise textures warp. Clip-space depth conventions and the near/far interval vary by API and projection setup, so the inequalities must match the active pipeline. Prerequisites
Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division Camera view and clip-space pipeline Barycentric coordinates and interpolation Triangle rasterization and coverage tests Depth buffering and visibility order GPU vertex specification

Source and navigation Teaching narrative: open the main explanation. Browse the University graphics and vision index. Additional chapter connections: Cameras, projection, and calibration; Rasterization, coverage, and depth; Homogeneous coordinates preserve the role of a location; A camera is another frame, so viewing uses its inverse. Caption/source records: P1-02, P3-05, P3-06, P3-12. Phase 11 camera development Clipping and perspective-correct interpolation preserve projective geometry, while texture filtering asks how much surface area maps to a pixel. Neighboring camera rays approximate the image-to-surface footprint. At grazing angles one pixel can cover a long, thin region; a center-only texel lookup may alias detail even when attributes interpolate correctly. Use footprint estimates to select mip levels or anisotropic filters, while respecting visibility edges where derivatives jump. Ray differentials aid sampling but do not replace clipping or multisample coverage. Source basis: PBRT differential-ray texture filtering. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review. Worked clip-plane trace beside the shader explanation For clip endpoints <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>6</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, the right-plane intersection uses homogeneous edge parameter <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>5</mn> </math>; interpolating the already divided endpoints would use <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>3</mn> </math>. The worked trace and pipeline figure also explain negative fourth components, the zero-divisor limit and declared depth conventions. This is used by the shader-stage teaching before program compilation and linking are discussed. Executable raster-state continuation The project now carries two complementary CPU witnesses. tools/labs/raster_reference_lab.cpp owns edge coverage, barycentrics, perspective-correct interpolation and depth ordering. tools/labs/raster_pipeline_state_lab.cpp continues the same pipeline through a homogeneous clip-plane intersection, an explicit four-sample coverage mask, stencil compare/pass update and premultiplied source-over blending. That separation is deliberate: clipping happens in homogeneous coordinates before divide-by-<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>w</mi> </math>; sample ownership happens after screen mapping; stencil/depth are stateful per-fragment/sample decisions; blending combines a surviving source with an existing destination. Treating all of them as “rasterization” without preserving these boundaries makes debugging nearly impossible.. Open Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Automatic differentiation and backpropagation — Automatic differentiation and backpropagation Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism Automatic differentiation evaluates derivatives by applying the chain rule to the operations in a program. Each operation has a local derivative rule; composing the rules gives the derivative of the complete computation without symbolically expanding it or approximating it by finite differences. Forward mode propagates a tangent perturbation and computes a Jacobian-vector product (JVP), useful when there are few inputs. Reverse mode propagates sensitivities from outputs back to inputs and computes a vector-Jacobian product (VJP), making gradients of one scalar loss with respect to millions of parameters practical. Backpropagation is reverse-mode differentiation through a neural network’s computation graph. It does not remove numerical problems: nondifferentiable operations require conventions, saturated activations can yield tiny gradients, and an incorrect graph or reduction yields an incorrect gradient. Gradients are local sensitivity information, not proof of a global optimum. Finite differences remain a useful small-scale check, but cancellation and step-size tradeoffs make them a poor training method. Phase 9–10 development Forward mode propagates an input tangent through local derivatives and computes a Jacobian-vector product. Reverse mode propagates an output sensitivity backward and computes a vector-Jacobian product. These are chain-rule evaluations on the operation graph, distinct from finite differences, which perturb inputs and can suffer cancellation. The reverse pass requires a valid reverse-topological order and storage that remains alive until propagation finishes. Differentiating a converged solution uses an implicit equation and its local Jacobian; it is not automatically the same as differentiating every solver iteration. Prerequisites
Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics Matrix multiplication and composition order Floating-point reassociation Derivative as a local linear map Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Reflection refraction and shading directions — Reflection refraction and shading directions Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Plane reflection reverses a direction’s normal component. Refraction scales its tangent component by the incident/transmitted index ratio and solves for a unit normal component. A negative computed discriminant indicates total internal reflection under the stated model. Half-vectors require normalized outward light/view directions. Incident <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0.6</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>0.8</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> reflects to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0.6</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0.8</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> across normal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Antiparallel light/view directions have no unique half-vector. Prerequisites
Projection rejection and scalar components — Removing an unwanted component creates residuals, tangent axes and mirror decompositions. Unit directions and safe normalization — Validated finite unit directions establish the preconditions for simplified geometry formulas.
Used by Later curriculum sources can deepen this same node; no future coverage is marked complete. - Lens optics and depth of field Recall and next depth Declare arrow and medium conventions before deriving formulas; distinguish direction geometry from optical energy. Full production proofs, target-specific integration and learner mastery require further evidence. Source and navigation Teaching narrative · Coverage and source gap · Evidence and limits · Dependency Map University course development Extend the existing direction note by separating geometric surface orientation from optical ray behavior. The normal vector is perpendicular to a local tangent plane; it determines the cosine term in diffuse shading and the directions of ideal reflection and refraction. For unit incident direction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math> and unit normal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>n</mi> </math>, specular reflection mirrors the direction about the normal, while refraction changes direction according to the ratio of refractive indices and may undergo total internal reflection. Direction conventions matter: some texts define incoming vectors toward the surface, others point away from it, so signs must be checked before applying formulas. A shading normal may differ from the true geometric normal, as in normal mapping, but it cannot change silhouette or visibility. Distinguish shading perturbations from geometry displacement, and use consistent normals when evaluating BRDFs, ray offsets, and medium transitions. Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Probability density and change of measure — Probability density and change of measure Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism A probability density describes probability per unit of a chosen measure, not probability at a point. A density <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>A</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> over area differs from a density <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>ω</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>ω</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> over solid angle. When a mapping changes variables, its Jacobian converts density so total probability remains one: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>B</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>A</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mi>d</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>d</mi> <mi>b</mi> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </math> in one dimension, with the determinant of the inverse Jacobian in multiple dimensions. In rendering, choosing a point on a light and using its direction from a shading point requires an area-to-solid-angle conversion involving distance squared and the light’s projected cosine. Estimator formulas are only correct when the sampling density and integral use the same measure. This concept prevents missing factors in importance sampling, environment-map sampling, and camera-lens integration. Phase 9–10 development A density is meaningful relative to a measure and its support; its value at a point is not itself an event probability. For a continuous scalar variable, an interval probability is the integral of the density over that interval. Under a differentiable one-to-one change of variables, the transformed density includes the absolute determinant of the inverse Jacobian. Values outside the transformed support have zero probability. A mixed law can contain both point masses and a continuous part, so one PDF alone cannot describe every distribution. When a renderer changes a surface-area density into a solid-angle density, the geometric Jacobian must preserve the same probability. Prerequisites

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Norms lengths and induced distances — Norms lengths and induced distances Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6 Definition and mechanism A norm is nonnegative, definite, absolutely homogeneous and satisfies the triangle inequality. It induces distance by taking the norm of a point difference. Coordinate-defined first, second and infinity norms answer different geometric questions. For <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, the three norms are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>7</mn> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>5</mn> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>4</mn> </math>. Squared length scales quadratically and is not itself a norm or induced metric. Prerequisites

M004 - Representation and rounding learning spine Prerequisites Dependent Why these steps are needed IEEE-754 floating point, Bit field Binary32 A 32-bit binary interchange format with one sign bit, eight exponent bits and 23 fraction bits. Normal precision is 24 bits; exponent bias is 127. Word 3F800000 has E=127,F=0 and means 1. Binary32 Binary64 A 64-bit binary interchange format with 1/11/52 fields, 53 significant normal bits and bias 1023. Normal exponent range is −1022 through 1023. Word 3FF0000000000000 means 1. Binary32 Exponent bias Normal exponents are encoded as unsigned E=e+B. Binary32 B=127, so exponent 3 stores 130. Field zero and all-ones are reserved; classify before subtracting bias. Binary32, Positional notation Significand and hidden bit The significand supplies significant digits; the exponent supplies scale. A normal binary value begins 1.f, so its leading one is implied, not stored. Binary32 fraction F contributes F/2^23; subnormals instead begin 0.f. Exponent bias, Significand and hidden bit, Hexadecimal Floating-point encoding and decoding Encoding chooses fields for a value; decoding classifies fields and reconstructs their meaning. 10.625 normalizes to 1.010101₂×2³, giving 412A0000. C1540000 decodes to −13.25. Binary32 Signed zero Exponent and fraction zero permit either sign. 00000000 and 80000000 compare numerically equal, but signbit and reciprocal distinguish them. Ordinary x<0 does not detect negative zero. Binary32 Floating-point infinities All-one exponent and zero fraction encode signed infinity. This is not maximum finite. Infinity minus itself is NaN; overflow’s result also depends on rounding direction. Binary32 NaNs and payloads All-one exponent with nonzero fraction encodes a non-numerical, unordered NaN. Quiet and signaling classes differ; fraction bits can carry payload information. Ordinary NaN equality is false; use isnan. Raw words can be classified without consuming signaling NaNs as floating values. Exponent bias, Significand and hidden bit Subnormals and gradual underflow Exponent zero and nonzero fraction remove the hidden one and hold the effective exponent at the normal minimum. Binary32 values are F×2^-149, connecting smoothly to 2^-126. Absolute spacing stays fixed while relative precision degrades. Significand and hidden bit Machine epsilon For these binary types epsilon is upward spacing at 1: 2^-23 for binary32 and 2^-52 for binary64. It is neither minimum positive value nor a physical threshold. Machine epsilon, Exponent bias, Subnormals and gradual underflow ULP and representable spacing A unit in the last place describes local spacing. Inside normal binade [2e,2(e+1)), p-bit precision gives spacing 2^(e-(p-1)). Immediately above 1 the binary32 gap is twice the gap below it. ULP and representable spacing Rounding to nearest ties to even Choose the nearest representable value; exactly halfway choose the even retained significand integer. At toy precision three bits, 1.125→1 and 1.375→1.5. std::round uses halfway-away-from-zero instead. ULP and representable spacing, Rounding to nearest ties to even Unit roundoff Under nearest binary rounding the conventional relative bound for normal-range results is u=2^-p, half upward epsilon. For binary32 this is 2^-24. The bound has range/rounding assumptions. Boolean algebra, Rounding to nearest ties to even Guard round and sticky bits Guard is first discarded bit, round the next, sticky ORs all remaining bits. With retained low bit L, nearest-even increments when G AND (R OR sticky OR L). Sticky summarizes any nonzero tail. Rounding to nearest ties to even Directed rounding modes Upward means toward positive infinity, downward toward negative infinity, and toward-zero truncates magnitude. Upward rounding of −2.1 to an integer gives −2, not −3. Directed rounding modes, NaNs and payloads Floating-point environment and compiler modes The environment includes rounding direction and exception status. Runtime mode changes can fail and must restore prior state. Strict compiler settings are needed; fast-math may discard required special-value or environment assumptions. IEEE-754 floating point, Subnormals and gradual underflow Floating-point exception flags Invalid, divide-by-zero, overflow, underflow and inexact are status conditions, not C++ throw exceptions. Exact subnormal results need not signal underflow. Flag/trap behavior depends on the environment. Subnormals and gradual underflow, Floating-point environment and compiler modes Flush-to-zero and denormals-are-zero FTZ flushes certain tiny results to zero; DAZ treats subnormal inputs as zero in supporting environments. They change gradual-underflow behavior. Cost and support are target/mode-specific. Fixed-width integer types, Interpretation contract, IEEE-754 floating point Bit casting and representation A same-size eligible bit_cast transfers representation, not numeric value. On the checked binary32 host, bit_cast<uint32_t>(1.0f)=3F800000, whereas a numeric cast gives 1. Pointer punning is not an equivalent legal operation. ULP and representable spacing, Signed zero, NaNs and payloads ULP distance policies Distance counts representable steps under a declared ordering/equality policy. The finite-only laboratory collapses both zeros to one key and rejects NaNs/infinities. Across negative minimum subnormal to positive minimum subnormal distance is two. Machine epsilon, ULP and representable spacing, Floating-point infinities, NaNs and payloads Numerical tolerance policies Tolerance is a task-chosen allowed discrepancy: absolute in original units, relative to scale, or representable-step based. Machine epsilon is not automatically a norm cutoff. Handle non-finite values and validate tolerances before formulas. IEEE-754 floating point, Floating-point infinities Robust norm and intermediate range A final representable answer can be lost to overflowing intermediates. Squaring 1e20f overflows before a finite norm could be formed. Scale by maximum component or use hypot to avoid unnecessary squared overflow. Numerical tolerance policies Conditioning and singularity Conditioning measures sensitivity to input perturbation. A=1e-4 I has determinant 1e-8 but condition number one in the 2-norm. Uniform scaling changes determinant magnitude without changing this conditioning measure. Signed zero, NaNs and payloads, Serialization, Bit casting and representation Floating-point canonicalization Canonicalization deliberately merges encodings: both zeros to positive zero, all NaNs to one quiet pattern. Raw preservation instead keeps sign/payload distinctions. Neither is universally correct; this is a file/hash contract choice. Directed rounding modes, Floating-point environment and compiler modes Interval arithmetic An interval encloses a possible exact value between lower and upper bounds. Correct outward rounding can preserve containment when the whole algorithm honors necessary assumptions. The first volume covers all Parts 1–100. Prerequisites explain the story’s dependencies; they do not require leaving the continuous volume to learn an essential definition. Representation choices and external contracts Prerequisites Dependent Why these steps are needed Two's complement, Interpretation contract Fixed-point representation A raw integer I represents I/S for an agreed positive scale S and units. With S=2^16, raw 212992 means 3.25. The integer has no built-in fractional point. Fixed-point representation Fixed-point range and resolution For signed N-bit raw storage and F fraction bits, step is 2^-F and the positive endpoint is (2(N-1)-1)/2F. Required step 0.001 and magnitude 1e6 in 32 bits allow F=10 or 11. Fixed-point representation, Minimum signed value, Arithmetic policies Fixed-point rescaling Raw multiplication changes scale S to S²; divide the wide product by S with a declared rounding rule. Raw division uses A*S/B. Check the destination after widening, and handle divisor zero and signed minima. Fixed-point representation, Absolute and relative error Affine quantization and zero point A positive step s, integer zero point z and bounded code q reconstruct x̂=s(q-z). Nearest encode uses clamp(round(x/s)+z). Half-step error assumes no clipping and ideal parameters. Affine quantization and zero point, Bit packing Groupwise quantization and metadata Local groups share a scale, improving adaptation at a metadata cost. Symmetric INT4 calibration maxAbs/7 reconstructs codes around [-7,7]; float scales add about 32/G bits per value for full groups. Quantization and compressed weights One-bit centroid quantization One sign label selects one of two row means. Row [-1,-3,2,4] reconstructs [-2,-2,3,3], with RMSE one. Two float32 centroids cost 64 additional bits per row. Affine quantization and zero point UNORM and SNORM UNORM decodes q/(2^n-1); UNORM8 code128 gives128/255. SNORM commonly clamps q/(2^(n-1)-1) at -1, so -128 and -127 both map to -1 for eight bits. IEEE-754 floating point, Rounding to nearest ties to even Binary16 IEEE binary16 has 1/5/10 fields, bias15 and11 normal precision bits. Word3E00 is1.5; maximum finite65504; normal minimum2^-14 and subnormal minimum2^-24. IEEE-754 floating point, Rounding to nearest ties to even Bfloat16 BF16 has1/8/7 fields, bias127 and8 normal precision bits. It keeps broad exponent range at coarse spacing2^-7 above1. A nearest-even conversion must handle NaNs separately from finite rounding. Unsigned modular arithmetic, Interpretation contract Offset-binary coding A bias turns signed levels into unsigned codes. For the source-shaped INT4 convention c=q+8, -3 becomes nibble0101, not the two’s-complement nibble1101. Absolute and relative error, Quantization and compressed weights Quantization error metrics For N>0, RMSE is sqrt(sum squared discrepancies/N), MAE is mean absolute discrepancy, and max error is the largest observed magnitude. Promote float operands before subtraction when measuring in double. Serialization, Bit casting and representation Binary format contracts A schema declares field widths/order, byte order, numeric representation, valid values, lengths, version, padding and identity policy. Magic identifies a candidate format; version chooses a schema, neither authenticates content. Binary format contracts, Unsigned modular arithmetic, Short-circuit evaluation Checked binary parsing Validate products before size calculation, ranges with offset≤size and length≤size-offset, and practical resource limits before allocation. Mapping/alignment does not itself establish valid typed object access. Bitwise XOR, Serialization Checksums CRCs and hashes Checksums/digests summarize specified bytes. Additive checksums miss reorderings; CRCs use GF(2) polynomial remainders and declared parameters. Cryptographic hashes need a trusted reference to support integrity claims against substitution. Checksums CRCs and hashes, Interpretation contract Integrity and authenticity Integrity compares content with a declared reference; authenticity requires a trust mechanism such as a MAC or signature. Replacing both file and untrusted digest defeats a simple hash comparison. Endianness, Bit casting and representation, Binary format contracts Memory dump interpretation Raw octets gain meaning from offsets, width, encoding and byte order. Bytes00 00 80 3F mean integer1065353216 or binary32 one under different little-endian contracts. A dump does not prove a typed object is live. Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: One-bit centroid quantization — One-bit centroid quantization Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C006 · Latest development: C006 Definition and mechanism One sign label selects one of two row means. Row [-1,-3,2,4] reconstructs [-2,-2,3,3], with RMSE one. Two float32 centroids cost 64 additional bits per row. Prerequisites
Quantization and compressed weights — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.
Used by Connect later dependent concepts here when their explanations use this mechanism. Recall and next depth Reconstruct the example and identify the condition that would invalidate it. Pending: Empty-side, zero and non-finite policies must be explicit in a production codec. Source and navigation Continuous teaching story · Source coverage ledger · Dependency Map Reconstruction depth One-bit centroid quantization does not merely store a sign. A group of source values is partitioned into two reconstruction levels, often centroids <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </math>, and each element stores one membership bit. Decoding is therefore <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">^</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>∈</mo> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math> If the centroids are fixed to symmetric values such as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo> </math>, metadata becomes cheaper but the representation loses the ability to follow asymmetric distributions. If they are fitted per group, metadata cost increases but reconstruction error can fall. The useful engineering quantity is total cost, not bits-per-weight in isolation: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mtext>effective bits/value</mtext> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <mtext>centroid metadata bits</mtext> <mtext>group size</mtext> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </math> Small groups adapt better but pay more metadata and may reduce SIMD efficiency. Large groups amortize metadata but force unrelated values to share two reconstruction levels. A correct implementation tests deterministic centroid selection, empty-cluster handling, tie policy, bit packing order, group tails, finite decoded values, and error against a declared metric. For inference, the important next question is whether the binary code can participate directly in a dot-product kernel or must be expanded first; that determines whether compression actually saves bandwidth.. Open One-bit centroid quantization in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Projection rejection and scalar components — Projection rejection and scalar components Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6 Definition and mechanism Projection onto a nonzero axis is the along-axis vector whose remainder is orthogonal. Rejection is the remainder. Signed scalar projection measures length; the projection coefficient multiplies the target axis and need not equal that length. For input <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and target <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, coefficient is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1.5</mn> </math>, scalar projection <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>3</mn> </math>, projection <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and rejection <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Scalars fields and real-number models — Scalars fields and real-number models Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6 Definition and mechanism A scalar is an element of the field used by a vector space. A field supports addition, multiplication and nonzero division under specified algebraic laws. The reals also supply order and completeness. Floating-point values approximate this model but do not form a mathematical field. An integer reciprocal need not be an integer; <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </math>. A real scalar can carry metres or seconds. A finite representation cannot preserve every real-number operation. Prerequisites The chapter establishes this foundation directly; no earlier accepted phase is assumed complete. Used by

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Quantization error metrics — Quantization error metrics Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C006 · Latest development: C006 Definition and mechanism For N>0, RMSE is sqrt(sum squared discrepancies/N), MAE is mean absolute discrepancy, and max error is the largest observed magnitude. Promote float operands before subtraction when measuring in double. Prerequisites
Absolute and relative error — supplies the representation or validity rule used above. Quantization and compressed weights — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.
Used by Connect later dependent concepts here when their explanations use this mechanism. Recall and next depth Reconstruct the example and identify the condition that would invalidate it. Pending: Representation error alone does not establish downstream task correctness. Source and navigation Continuous teaching story · Source coverage ledger · Dependency Map A metric must match what the consumer loses Quantization error is the difference <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>e</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">^</mo> </mover> </mrow> </math> between source and reconstruction, but one scalar summary cannot answer every engineering question. Mean squared error emphasizes large deviations; mean absolute error is less sensitive to outliers; maximum absolute error exposes worst-case bounds; relative error becomes useful when scale varies but is unstable near zero. For tensors, per-tensor MSE can hide one badly damaged channel or group. Diagnostics should often include per-group distributions, saturation counts, scale histograms, and downstream task error. A quantizer that minimizes weight MSE is not guaranteed to minimize model-output error because layers amplify directions differently. Signal metrics also depend on representation. Comparing gamma-encoded RGB with ordinary squared error is not the same as comparing linear-light energy. Normals may need angular error rather than component MSE. A useful quantization benchmark therefore reports storage cost together with several reconstruction metrics and one consumer-level metric. The metric is part of the experiment hypothesis, not a decorative number added after compression.. Open Quantization error metrics in Volume 1

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Expectation, covariance, and dependence — Expectation, covariance, and dependence Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism Expectation is the probability-weighted average of a random quantity, and variance is the expected squared deviation from that average. Covariance measures how two centered quantities vary together; correlation scales it to a unitless linear-association measure. For a random vector, the covariance matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite because every directional quadratic form equals a variance. Zero covariance does not usually imply independence, except under special joint Gaussian conditions. Conditional expectation and total-variance identities decompose uncertainty into within-group spread and variation between group means. These moments drive Monte Carlo error analysis, Gaussian geometry, and linear uncertainty propagation. An empirical covariance depends on sample convention and denominator; Bessel correction concerns unbiased population-variance estimation under IID sampling, not a universal change to descriptive covariance. Prerequisites
Probability spaces, events, and conditioning Random variables and probability laws
Used by

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Newton and quasi-Newton optimization — Newton and quasi-Newton optimization Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism Newton’s method builds a local quadratic model of an objective from its gradient and Hessian, then solves for the model’s stationary point. Near a well-conditioned solution with suitable smoothness and curvature, it can converge faster than gradient descent. Away from that regime, the Hessian may be indefinite, poorly scaled, or a poor model over the proposed step. Line searches and trust regions control step acceptance. Quasi-Newton methods such as BFGS estimate curvature from successive parameter and gradient changes, avoiding repeated exact Hessian construction. Their guarantees depend on assumptions and update safeguards. Optimization should monitor objective change, gradient norm, step size, constraints, and numerical failures; a small step alone can indicate stagnation rather than success. The method’s result is a local solution unless global structure proves more. Prerequisites
Hessians and local curvature Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Reservoir resampling and ReSTIR — Reservoir resampling and ReSTIR Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Reservoir sampling keeps a compact candidate for a weighted distribution without storing every sample. When candidate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math> has target weight <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math>, maintain a running weight sum and replace the stored candidate with probability proportional to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math>; the reservoir records enough normalization information to estimate the desired integral without bias under stated assumptions. ReSTIR reuses candidates across pixels and frames, which is valuable when direct lighting has many possible lights or paths but only a few can be evaluated per pixel. Reuse requires correcting for the source and target distributions, accounting for visibility changes, and managing temporal history. If weights or normalization are wrong, the image may be biased; stale reuse causes trails or light leaks when geometry or illumination moves. The method reduces expensive samples rather than making sampling free. It depends on a valid estimator, careful normalization, and an understanding of whether correlated reused samples preserve the intended expectation. Prerequisites
Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance Sampling aliasing and reconstruction Temporal reprojection and history validation Reflectance and rendering equation
Used by
Numerical integration and Monte Carlo estimation

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Pointer arithmetic and provenance — Pointer arithmetic and provenance Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C008 Definition and mechanism M008 adds null/object/one-past distinctions, same-array representable subtraction and round-trip limits. Provenance proposals are research, not adopted C++23 rules; byte inspection differs from arbitrary typed access. A scalar member behaves as a one-element array for pointer arithmetic, not as an array containing adjacent sibling members. &x+1 can be a one-past pointer but cannot be dereferenced to access y. Actual array storage supports traversal; a span only views an already-valid range. Layout/size assertions do not authorize sibling traversal. A pointer is a typed access path constrained by array bounds, alignment, and object lifetime, not merely an integer. Within an array, p+i advances i elements; one-past is permitted for traversal but not dereference. Byte views inspect representations; uintptr_t, when provided, is an integer conversion facility, not permission to access arbitrary storage. Prerequisites
Addresses and virtual memory — Mappings give numeric locations their process-specific storage identity. Storage duration and object lifetime — Access requires an object and backing storage that are still valid.
Used by

Explain p+1 for int versus byte and why a numeric address is insufficient. Pending: Full lifetime replacement, ownership/concurrency policies and cross-target ABI experiments; the opening examples do not establish those later guarantees.
