This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Local rigidity and mesh orientation fields — Local rigidity and mesh orientation fields Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) deformation seeks vertex positions that change as little as possible from a preferred local rigid transform. For each vertex neighborhood, fit a rotation to the deformed edge vectors, then minimize residuals between transformed rest edges and current edges. Alternating between local rotations and a global position solve makes a nonlinear shape-editing problem tractable, but the result depends on constraints, initialization, mesh quality, and rotation fitting. Instant Meshes uses direction or orientation fields over a surface to guide a quad-dominant remeshing; field singularities encode where a globally consistent direction cannot exist. A mesh’s half-edge connectivity, boundary structure, and orientation determine valid neighborhoods and field transport. Poor triangles, seams, boundary conditions, or inconsistent orientation can create artifacts. ARAP is a local preservation objective, not exact rigidity of the whole shape; a direction field guides topology but does not uniquely determine a good mesh without sizing and feature constraints. Prerequisites
Half-edge mesh connectivity Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure Subdivision surface masks Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics Cross products and oriented area
Used by

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Implicit differentiation and parameter sensitivities — Implicit differentiation and parameter sensitivities Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism Implicit differentiation obtains how a solution changes when it is defined by an equation rather than an explicit formula. If a state satisfies F(y,θ)=0 and the Jacobian with respect to y is invertible, differentiating gives dy/dθ=−(∂F/∂y)⁻¹(∂F/∂θ). This can differentiate equilibrium states, constrained optima, and roots without unrolling every solver iteration. For a converged optimizer, differentiating stationarity and constraint conditions yields sensitivity equations, but active-set changes, nonunique solutions, singular Jacobians, and imperfect convergence complicate the result. Continuous sensitivity equations propagate derivatives alongside an ODE; adjoint methods can reduce cost when there are many parameters and few scalar outputs. These are modeling tools with assumptions, not a guarantee that every algorithmic branch is differentiable. Prerequisites
Automatic differentiation and backpropagation Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics ODE integration and stability

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Ray differentials and camera sampling measures — Ray differentials and camera sampling measures Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 Definition and mechanism A camera sample selects a film location and usually a shutter time, then maps that sample to a weighted ray or path contribution. Ray differentials approximate how neighboring pixel samples change the generated ray; after intersection they estimate the surface footprint covered by a pixel and help choose a texture filter level. A sampling measure states which quantity is sampled and therefore which probability density belongs in a Monte Carlo estimator; area, solid angle, image-plane area, and discrete pixel measures are not interchangeable without a Jacobian. Example: two adjacent pixels generate rays whose intersection points span a large patch on a distant oblique surface, so filtering should average that footprint rather than use a single high-frequency texel. Differential rays are local first-order approximations and can fail at discontinuities or complex lens mappings; the weight and PDF must match the camera model and chosen measure. Example: For a pinhole camera, offset the raster sample by one pixel in x and y, generate neighboring rays, and intersect them with a textured plane; the resulting parallelogram estimates the pixel footprint for texture filtering. Assumptions: Differentials approximate nearby rays locally and are not exact at visibility or lens discontinuities.; Importance weights/PDFs are valid only when defined in the same measure as the estimator. Prerequisites
Camera view and clip-space pipeline Visual angle and calibrated rays Lens optics and depth of field
Used by
A camera model must close the loop Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Inverse, rejection, and importance sampling — Inverse, rejection, and importance sampling Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism Sampling transforms convert simpler random inputs into a target law. Inverse-CDF sampling maps a uniform value through a quantile function; rejection sampling accepts proposal draws according to a bounded target-to-proposal ratio; importance sampling estimates an integral by dividing each sampled integrand by the actual proposal density. Each method requires correct support and endpoint handling. Importance sampling is unbiased when the proposal covers every contributing region and the weighted contribution is integrable; finite variance additionally requires the integral of f²/p to be finite. Rejection sampling needs a valid finite envelope. Discrete floating-point inputs can hit boundaries that have zero probability in an ideal continuous model. Report the density with its measure and use the same measure in the estimator. A proposal that misses target support cannot be repaired by a larger weight. Prerequisites
Random variables and probability laws Probability density and change of measure Stateful pseudorandom generators and stream state
Used by
Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Quaternion rotation and double cover — Quaternion rotation and double cover Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase7 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism For a unit quaternion q, the sandwich q(0,v)conjugate(q) rotates v. q and minus q give the same physical rotation. Every nonzero quaternion also rotates without scale if its true inverse is used; substituting conjugate for inverse off the unit sphere scales by the squared norm. Reconstruction cue: The scalar-first quaternion (sqrt(1/2),0,0,sqrt(1/2)) rotates the X axis to Y. Prerequisites
Quaternion algebra and Hamilton product
Used by
Quaternion matrix and axis-angle conversion Quaternion interpolation and shortest paths
Recall and next depth Reconstruct the example, state its conventions and find an input that violates its preconditions. Deeper algorithms and measured production performance remain separate from the present model. Source and navigation Continuous explanation · Coverage and source gap · Sources and verification University course development Extend the existing quaternion note with interpolation and sign handling in animation. A unit quaternion represents a 3D rotation, but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <mi>q</mi> </math> encode the same physical orientation. If two endpoint quaternions have a negative dot product, negate one endpoint before interpolation so the path follows the shorter arc on the unit four-dimensional sphere. Linear interpolation followed by normalization is inexpensive and often adequate for close orientations; spherical linear interpolation travels at constant angular speed for widely separated rotations. Quaternion interpolation acts on orientation, while translation and scale need their own rules. This matters in camera paths and articulated characters: interpolating four components without handling the double cover can create an unnecessary long spin, while interpolating Euler angles can encounter a gimbal singularity. Validate unit length after operations subject to floating-point drift. Coordinate frames, transformations, and pose · Scene graphs and articulated geometry · Animation curves and motion paths. Open Quaternion rotation and double cover in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Conditioning and singularity — Conditioning and singularity Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C004 · Latest development: Phase7 Definition and mechanism Conditioning measures sensitivity to input perturbation. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>4</mn> </mrow> </msup> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </math> has determinant <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>8</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math> but condition number one in the 2-norm. Uniform scaling changes determinant magnitude without changing this conditioning measure. Phase 7 develops <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>κ</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>A</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mi>A</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <msup> <mi>A</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> </math>, near-parallel-column sensitivity, pivoted elimination and inverse residuals. Equal determinants can conceal very different stretch ratios: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>diag</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>10</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>10</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>diag</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>20</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> both have determinant <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>20</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math> but conditions one and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mn>20</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>. Full worked sensitivity example. Subtraction of nearby inputs exposes input uncertainty relative to a small difference. Sensitivity belongs to the problem; exact subtraction of stored operands cannot recover information lost when those inputs were rounded. Prerequisites

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Time integrators and symplectic updates — Time integrators and symplectic updates Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism A time integrator turns a differential equation into a discrete state update. Explicit Euler uses the current slope; midpoint and Runge–Kutta methods combine several slope evaluations to improve local accuracy; semi-implicit Euler updates velocity before position and can behave better for mechanical systems. Symplectic methods preserve the geometric structure of Hamiltonian dynamics, often keeping long-run energy error bounded rather than allowing systematic drift. No method is universally best: order, stability region, cost, conservation, and stiffness all matter. A higher formal order does not guarantee better behavior at an unsuitable step size or under discontinuous forces. Compare integrators on the same problem, step policy, and error target. Update order is part of the algorithm: changing it can change stability and physical behavior, not merely code style. Prerequisites
ODE initial-value problems and stiffness
Used by
ODE integration and stability

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Exposure and sensor response — Exposure and sensor response Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism A camera sensor converts arriving photons into electrical measurements. Exposure depends on scene radiance, lens transmission, aperture, shutter duration, and sensor sensitivity; changing these settings trades motion blur, depth of field, noise, and saturation. A pixel integrates light over a finite area and exposure interval before quantization. Sensor wells have finite capacity, so highlights clip, while low photon counts have shot noise and readout adds electronic noise. ISO gain amplifies the signal and its noise rather than collecting additional photons. The recorded raw values are not yet display colors: white balance, color transforms, tone curves, and transfer encoding turn measurements into an image. A camera model must distinguish photon capture, sensor response, and display rendering to explain dynamic range and exposure choices. Prerequisites
Lens optics and depth of field Color encoding and linear-light operations
Used by
Worlds, Images and Inference
Full teaching explanation Exposure, sensors, and dynamic range · Photographic workflow and integrated decisions. Open Exposure and sensor response in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Depth buffering and visibility order — Depth buffering and visibility order Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism A depth buffer stores the nearest depth seen so far for each image sample. When rasterizing a fragment, compare its depth with the stored value; if it is closer, update both depth and color, otherwise discard it. This per-sample test resolves opaque visibility without sorting all triangles. Perspective projection maps view-space depth nonlinearly, so the near and far clipping planes affect how floating-point precision is distributed. If they span an unnecessarily huge ratio, nearly coplanar surfaces may quantize to equal or inconsistent depths and flicker as the camera moves; this is z-fighting. Alpha-blended surfaces need additional ordering or order-independent methods because color composition is not commutative. Depth establishes visibility, while transparency determines how multiple visible layers contribute. Prerequisites
Triangle rasterization and coverage tests Camera view and clip-space pipeline
Used by
Worlds, Images and Inference Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation Hardware depth-buffer linearization ## Full teaching explanation
Rasterization, coverage, and depth · Textures and surface detail Phase 11 camera development Depth gives ordering or camera-relative distance under a specific projection convention; it does not identify the surface that produced a sample. Reprojecting old color and depth can place history behind a newly visible surface. Validate with current depth, normal, object identity, or neighborhood checks; reject disocclusions and large reprojection errors. Reversed-Z and nonlinear perspective depth require consistent reconstruction before threshold comparisons. Valid visibility does not guarantee photometric stability after lighting, exposure, or material changes. Link depth semantics to temporal history validation. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.. Open Depth buffering and visibility order in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Sampling quality: stratification, quasi-Monte Carlo, and blue noise — Sampling quality: stratification, quasi-Monte Carlo, and blue noise Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism Sampling quality concerns the arrangement of points across dimensions used by an estimator, not only each coordinate’s one-dimensional histogram. Stratification partitions a domain and allocates points across cells, reducing large gaps for suitable integrands. Quasi-Monte Carlo sequences such as Sobol aim for low discrepancy and often improve integration of smooth, structured functions, though their samples are dependent and error estimates differ from IID Monte Carlo. Blue-noise point sets suppress low-frequency clumping while retaining local separation; they are useful in image sampling and spatial placement but do not automatically minimize every integral’s variance. Scrambling, domain mapping, dimensional ordering, and discontinuities affect performance. Compare methods against a clear target function and measure. The supplied probability narrative introduces stratification and Sobol but not blue-noise constructions; that part is an explicit teaching addition, not a received source claim. Prerequisites
Stateless keyed sampling and reproducibility Sampling aliasing and reconstruction Uniform shuffling without replacement ## Used by Antialiasing and sample allocation Latin-hypercube sampling ## Full teaching explanation Phase 10 teaching section Visual Recall/10 - Probability and Monte Carlo - Visual Recall.md · visual recall

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Reproducible numerical benchmarking — Reproducible numerical benchmarking Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism A useful numerical benchmark separates sample-level variability from run-level variability and pairs competing methods on the same inputs or seeds. Record the algorithm, precision, compiler/runtime settings, sample count, seed or keyed input, warm-up policy, timing method, and error metric. Compare distributions or paired differences rather than a single favorable run. A speed improvement is meaningful only if accuracy and failure rates remain acceptable for the target workload. For Monte Carlo methods, repeat independent runs and report uncertainty; for deterministic solvers, use analytical or manufactured solutions and measure convergence. Reproducibility is an experimental contract, not merely a fixed random seed. If the workload is stochastic, compare paired seeds and report both runtime and error distributions. Prerequisites
Numerical reproducibility Confidence intervals and sequential evidence Robust summaries and error metrics Numerical error budgets Convergence order and Richardson extrapolation Latin-hypercube sampling

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Stereo correspondence and epipolar geometry — Stereo correspondence and epipolar geometry Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Stereo reconstruction uses two or more views to infer depth from corresponding image features. A 3D point and the two camera centers define an epipolar plane; its intersection with each image plane is an epipolar line. Thus a feature in one image should match along a one-dimensional line in the other, reducing a 2D search to a constrained search. With calibrated cameras, triangulation intersects the two viewing rays; noise means they are skew, so estimate the 3D point minimizing reprojection or ray distance. Depth uncertainty grows rapidly when the viewing rays are nearly parallel, which happens for distant points or small baselines. Rectification rotates images so epipolar lines become horizontal scanlines. Occlusion, repetitive texture, and calibration error can still produce mismatches, so confidence and consistency checks are essential. Prerequisites
Camera calibration and bundle adjustment Barycentric coordinates and interpolation

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Confidence intervals and sequential evidence — Confidence intervals and sequential evidence Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism A confidence interval is a procedure with repeated-sample coverage under stated assumptions; it is not a posterior probability assigned to a fixed parameter. A normal interval for a mean uses a known population standard deviation or an approximation justified by the central limit theorem. With unknown scale and IID normal observations, the Student t distribution accounts for estimating the standard deviation. Heavy tails, sample dependence, multiple comparisons, and optional stopping can invalidate simple textbook guarantees. Adaptive algorithms that stop when a fixed-sample interval looks narrow need sequentially valid methods or a separately justified stopping rule. Report the target, sampling unit, dependence structure, estimator bias, interval procedure, stopping policy, and independent-run count. A narrow interval around a biased estimator measures precision about its expectation, not correctness of the target. Prerequisites
Common probability distributions and their assumptions Expectation, covariance, and dependence Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Axial depth and Euclidean range — Axial depth and Euclidean range Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11 Definition and mechanism Axial depth measures distance along the camera’s forward axis; Euclidean range measures distance from the camera centre along the viewing ray. With a right-handed view frame looking along <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <mi>Z</mi> </math>, positive axial depth is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>d</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mi>z</mi> </math>, while range is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>r</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msqrt> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mi>y</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mi>z</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </msqrt> </math>. They agree only on the optical axis. For a unit ray direction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> </math> with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>z</mi> </msub> <mo><</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>, a range measurement converts to axial depth as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>d</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mi>r</mi> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>z</mi> </msub> </math>. A range sensor and a perspective depth buffer may therefore encode different quantities. Applying a depth-buffer formula directly to a range image distorts reconstructed geometry away from the image centre. At view point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>12</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, axial depth is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>12</mn> </math> while range is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>13</mn> </math>, a visible distinction off-axis. This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division — Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Phase 7 derives the affine block matrix, distinguishes a singular affine map from an invertible frame, and traces model → view → homogeneous clip → NDC using a declared projection. The worked figure keeps the divisor visible and checks the chosen near/far depth endpoints. An affine homogeneous point has last coordinate one; a direction has zero. Nonzero common scale defines projective equivalence, while dehomogenization divides by a nonzero final component. Clip representatives and projective classes have related but distinct semantics. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>6</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> describe one finite projective point. NDC normalization standardizes ranges, not vector length. Prerequisites
Vectors coordinates and affine points — Point, displacement and coordinate roles determine which geometric operations are meaningful.
Used by
Linear affine and projective transformations
Later curriculum sources can deepen this same node; no future coverage is marked complete. - Ray-triangle intersection - Camera calibration and bundle adjustment
Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation Position reconstruction from depth Camera gauge freedoms and observability
Recall and next depth Explain why perspective division is nonlinear and why clipping must precede casual division. Full production proofs, target-specific integration and learner mastery require further evidence. Source and navigation Teaching narrative · Coverage and source gap · Evidence and limits · Dependency Map University course development Extend the existing account with the geometric reason for the final divide. A 3D point is stored as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>; after multiplying by a projective matrix it becomes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>X</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Z</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>W</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Dividing the first three components by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>W</mi> </math> maps the homogeneous representative to ordinary coordinates. Any nonzero scalar multiple of a homogeneous vector represents the same point, which is why this division is meaningful. For a perspective camera, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>W</mi> </math> is chosen to depend on depth, so apparent size shrinks with distance. A direction has homogeneous coordinate zero and is not translated like a point. Projection matrices encode the camera frustum before division; afterward, a viewport transform scales and shifts normalized coordinates to pixels and commonly flips the vertical axis because image rows increase downward. Keep clipping before division to avoid unstable behavior around <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>W</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>. Coordinate frames, transformations, and pose · Cameras, projection, and calibration Phase 11 camera development Homogeneous image coordinates represent a ray up to nonzero scale; perspective division produces normalized image coordinates. Monocular reconstruction has a separate physical scale gauge: multiplying all scene points and camera translations by the same positive factor preserves projections. Do not confuse representational scale with unknown metric scale. A known object dimension, baseline, or depth measurement can anchor metres; normalizing a homogeneous vector cannot. This assumes calibrated perspective projection without an external scale prior. The distinction explains why a numerically precise reconstruction can still lack physical units. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.. Open Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division in Volume 2

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: 10 - Probability and Monte Carlo - Visual Recall — Probability and uncertainty — visual recall
Shortest route: start with a model of outcomes, then ask what distribution the computer actually sampled, how it weighted each sample, and what evidence supports the estimate. Reconstruct the chain (Ω, F, P) describes outcomes, measurable events, and their probabilities. A random variable maps outcomes into numbers; a random vector preserves their joint behavior. A PMF assigns point mass to discrete values; a PDF gives density relative to a stated measure; a CDF accumulates probability and exists even when no PDF does. Conditioning changes the information available. Independence means joint probability factors, not merely that events are disjoint. Bayes reverses the conditioning direction by multiplying likelihood by prior and normalizing over alternatives. Expectation is a probability-weighted center. Variance is mean squared spread. Covariance records coupled variation; correlation divides it by both standard deviations but only captures linear association. For a vector, covariance is symmetric PSD because aᵀΣa = Var(aᵀX) ≥ 0. Bernoulli describes one binary outcome; binomial counts IID Bernoulli successes. Uniform has constant density in its declared measure. Gaussian describes a quadratic-distance bell shape. Exponential waiting times are memoryless; Poisson counts belong to the corresponding constant-rate process. A multivariate Gaussian’s covariance sets ellipse/ellipsoid orientation and scale. The computational chain is: seed/state or keyed input → finite random bits → sample transform → actual PDF and measure → weighted contribution f(X)/p(X) → average → uncertainty/error report Every arrow carries assumptions. A wrong PDF or measure can bias the result. A low-variance estimator can still be biased. Correlated observations change the standard error. Confidence intervals do not repair a wrong expectation. Formula prompts Prompt Reconstruct Conditioning P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B); chain rule multiplies successive conditional probabilities. Bayes P(H|E)=P(E|H)P(H)/ΣᵢP(E|Hᵢ)P(Hᵢ). Expected transform E[g(X)] = Σg(x)p(x) or ∫g(x)p(x)dx. Variance/covariance Var(X)=E[X²]−E[X]²; Cov(X,Y)=E[XY]−E[X]E[Y]. Linear propagation E[AX+b]=Aμ+b; Cov(AX+b)=AΣAᵀ; local nonlinear approximation uses JΣJᵀ. Importance estimate I=∫f dx=Eₚ[f(X)/p(X)]; average contributions and divide by the actual sampling density. Monte Carlo error IID finite-variance mean has Var(Ȳ)=σ²/N, SE=σ/√N; four times samples halves SE. Estimator quality MSE = variance + bias². Bessel/Welford Unbiased sample variance uses M₂/(n−1); update with δ=x−μ, μ←μ+δ/n, M₂←M₂+δ(x−μ). Error metrics MSE squares; RMSE returns original units; MAE uses absolute error; relative metrics fail or need policy near zero. Fast error checks
Does a density integrate to one in the stated coordinate measure? Is its unit inverse measure? Are the samples distributed according to the PDF used in the weight? Is a stated confidence interval fixed-sample, and are IID/normal or approximation assumptions plausible? Is covariance symmetric PSD? Does singular mean invalid, or valid but lower-rank? Are sample and population variance being confused? Is a single run being mistaken for evidence of variance reduction? Is a “Gaussian” a normalized probability model or merely a rendering kernel?
Targeted backlinks
stable numerics conditioning coordinate changes positive definiteness covariance eigenstructure
Parts covered by supplied sources: 901–1000. The numerical continuation and figure index below complete this received phase. Source-provided recall and compact formula reference Supplied concise recall summary The mathematical core is the probability space <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi data-mjx-variant="-tex-calligraphic" mathvariant="script">F</mi> </mrow> <mo>,</mo> <mi>P</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, random variables defined on that space, and probability laws for their values. Conditional probability changes the reference information. Independence is a factorization property. PMFs assign masses to discrete values, while PDFs assign density relative to a measure. CDFs accumulate probability and exist for every real-valued random variable. Expected value describes the weighted centre. Variance describes squared spread. Covariance describes coupled spread. Correlation standardizes covariance but does not measure every form of dependence. Bernoulli models one binary trial. Binomial models the count of successes in independent identically distributed Bernoulli trials. Uniform models constant density over a region. Gaussian models a particular smooth bell-shaped distribution. Exponential models memoryless waiting times. Poisson models event counts under its defining assumptions. A multivariate Gaussian combines mean, covariance, and correlations into a joint distribution. Positive-definite covariance permits a full-dimensional nonsingular Gaussian density. Singular PSD covariance describes a distribution confined to a lower-dimensional affine subspace. Key engineering invariants: all probabilities are valid and normalized; PDF units match the integration measure; covariance is symmetric PSD; Gaussian density evaluation avoids unnecessary inversion; nonfinite inputs and singular cases are explicit; sampling tests use statistical tolerances rather than exact equality. solve z=inverse(L)(x-mu); then Mahalanobis squared distance is z transpose z. A singular covariance is supported on a lower-dimensional affine subspace. Rebuild the numerical witness. Six figures
F10-1. Ordered outcomes and the exact two-dice sum PMF. The supplied lesson already derives this example; the figure is a visual check of the 36 ordered pairs. PMF numerators sum to 36 and P(S=7)=1/6.
F10-2. Zero covariance need not mean independence. For standard normal X, Cov(X,X squared)=0 by symmetry although X and X squared are dependent. Sample covariance is a finite-run witness.
F10-3. Uniform area sampling requires a square-root radial transform. The theoretical mean radius is 2/3 for uniform area in the unit disk and 1/2 for uniform radius; plotted sample means are finite-run illustrations.
F10-4. Monte Carlo random error and a fixed bias floor. For the stated integral, unbiased RMSE falls with sample count while the biased estimator retains its offset.
F10-5. A matched importance proposal can make contributions constant. For the stated nonnegative integrand and support, the matched proposal gives constant contributions; uniform-proposal variance is 4/45. This does not generalize to arbitrary signed integrands.
F10-6. A full-period toy LCG can still have a simple low-bit pattern. For m=16, a=5, c=1, all 16 states are visited but the least-significant bit alternates. Full period does not imply good multidimensional quality. The keyed-input sketch indicates deterministic indexing only: a different key does not establish statistical independence or collision freedom. State arithmetic assumptions (normal/subnormal, overflow, rounding mode) and data scale. Check both residual/backward error and conditioning before interpreting forward accuracy. Verify interpolation range, boundary policy, and parameter units. Separate discretization, truncation, roundoff, and sampling error. Fix a reproducible reduction tree or record seed, sample design, and uncertainty. Test exact identities, invariants, edge cases, convergence order, and randomized strata.

Numerical reliability figures and their explanations
N10-7 · Summation is an algorithm, not just a plus sign — Exact real sum is 10000. The three-term counterexample shows why Kahan is not an exact-arithmetic guarantee. Strict IEEE-style evaluation is assumed; reassociation can invalidate compensation. N10-8 · More polynomial degree does not guarantee a better picture — Both interpolants match every node. Their behaviour between nodes differs. Chebyshev extrema reduce this example’s endpoint oscillation; this comparison is not a universal interpolation error bound. N10-9 · Bézier and Hermite can tell the same curve story — Use Hermite tangents 3(P1−P0) and 3(P3−P2) for this cubic Bézier curve. The control polygon bounds the curve through nonnegative weights summing to one; inner control points need not lie on the curve. N10-10 · A root solver needs both progress and a safety argument — The error comparison uses cos(x)−x with specified starting values. Bisection has a shrinking bracket; Newton and secant need additional hypotheses. The plotting floor is explicitly shown rather than interpreted as continuing convergence. N10-11 · Arbitrary sample counts need full-domain support — Left: choosing the first five of nine equal cells and averaging equally gives E[y] = 0.3, while the uniform-square value is 0.5. Right: one point per marginal bin is a midpoint illustration; randomized LHS jitters and permutes appropriately, and is not full multidimensional stratification. N10-12 · Algebraically equal formulas can have unequal numerical error — The reference uses 90-digit Decimal arithmetic and compares binary64 formulas for b from 100 to 10¹⁶. This bounded example illustrates cancellation, not a complete robust quadratic solver.

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Basis coordinates and dimension — Basis coordinates and dimension Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase7 Definition and mechanism Phase 7 stores basis images as matrix columns and derives coordinate conversion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mi>v</mi> <msub> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> <mi>C</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>C</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mi>B</mi> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mi>v</mi> <msub> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> <mi>B</mi> </msub> </math>. The endpoint bases and whether motion is active or passive determine the product; row-major storage does not. Reconstruction and active/passive example. A basis is an ordered independent spanning set. Independence makes coordinates unique; spanning makes every vector reachable. Dimension counts basis elements over the chosen field, not stored components or bytes. A basis change alters coordinates without necessarily moving the physical vector. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, so its slanted-basis coordinates are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. A plane inside three-dimensional coordinates still has dimension two. Prerequisites
Vector spaces subspaces and span — Reachability and closure establish the spanning and independence questions.
Used by
Matrices as linear maps and basis images Norms lengths and induced distances — Builds on this mechanism in the connected geometry story. Gram matrices and coordinate metrics — Builds on this mechanism in the connected geometry story. Covectors linear functionals and normal transforms — Builds on this mechanism in the connected geometry story. Linear systems and fundamental subspaces — Extends this foundation into linear-systems and decomposition analysis. Spline bases and curve evaluation Additive energy and approximate structure Exceptional projections and dimension ## Recall and next depth
Separate passive coordinate change from active transformation and explain near-dependent basis sensitivity. Full production proofs, target-specific integration and learner mastery require further evidence. Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Stable probability normalization and log-sum-exp — Stable probability normalization and log-sum-exp Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism To normalize nonnegative weights, divide each by their sum; direct summation can overflow even when the normalized probabilities are representable. Scale by the largest weight before summing. For log weights <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math>, compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>m</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>log</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>−</mo> <mi>m</mi> </mrow> </msup> </math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>m</mi> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">max</mo> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math>. Subtracting the maximum prevents exponential overflow, and the result can be used to form softmax probabilities. This assumes at least one finite, valid weight and requires an explicit policy for all-zero, negative, NaN, or infinite inputs. Underflow of very small normalized probabilities is a separate concern from overflow; do not silently equate zero after underflow with mathematically impossible. For log weights <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1000</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1001</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1000</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, subtracting <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1001</mn> </math> keeps exponentials bounded while leaving the normalized probabilities unchanged. Prerequisites

Used by

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Convolution and filter footprints — Convolution and filter footprints Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Convolution combines shifted values with a weighting kernel; its spectrum multiplies transfer functions. Pixel footprints and boundary policies define what is averaged. A separable Gaussian uses two 1D passes; unpadded DFT filtering wraps circularly. Prerequisites
Continuous signals and discrete samples — Filtering/frequency analysis operates on a declared domain and its samples. Fourier analysis and spectral phase — Frequency and phase reveal transfer, sampling ambiguity and structural loss.
Used by
PSF OTF and MTF Multiscale texture filtering Optical flow and time to contact Edge localization and subpixel contours Template matching and distance transforms PDE fields and discrete Laplacians Attention and visual transformers Learned image features and CNNs ## Recall and next depth
Derive the three-tap filter’s gain and constant preservation. Pending: implementation cost, padding and spatially varying kernels. Written coverage is not a claim of learner mastery or accepted numbered-curriculum progress. Source and navigation Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map University course development Extend the current convolution note from a sliding kernel to image formation and resampling. A pixel integrates incoming image energy over a finite footprint; point sampling is only an approximation to that area integral. Convolution combines nearby values with weights whose spatial support is the kernel footprint, and its Fourier transform describes which spatial frequencies survive. Before reducing resolution, low-pass filtering suppresses frequencies the coarser grid cannot represent. In texture mapping, the screen-to-texture Jacobian maps a nearly square screen pixel to a texture-space parallelogram. If the two singular directions have very different lengths, an isotropic mip level blurs one direction too much; anisotropic filters take extra samples along the long axis. This same footprint reasoning links pixel reconstruction, antialiasing, texture filtering, and sensor blur without treating them as unrelated tricks. Sampling continuous signals and image formation · Image sampling, filtering, and efficient reconstruction · Textures and surface detail. Open Convolution and filter footprints in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Determinants orientation and volume — Determinants orientation and volume Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase7 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism A square matrix determinant measures oriented volume scale. Zero means rank loss; sign records orientation reversal. Its magnitude depends on scale and is not a standalone measure of numerical conditioning. Reconstruction cue: Uniform tiny scaling can have tiny determinant and condition number one. Prerequisites
Cross products and oriented area Matrices as linear maps and basis images
Used by
Matrix inversion pivoting and residuals Polar decomposition — Extends this foundation into linear-systems and decomposition analysis. ## Recall and next depth
Reconstruct the example, state its conventions and find an input that violates its preconditions. Deeper algorithms and measured production performance remain separate from the present model. Source and navigation Continuous explanation · Coverage and source gap · Sources and verification University course development Computational geometry often decides whether points are left or right of a directed line, whether three points are collinear, or whether a point lies inside a circle. These decisions reduce to determinant signs. For points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>c</mi> </math> in 2D, the signed area determinant classifies orientation. If its exact value is near zero, floating-point rounding can change the sign and make neighboring algorithms disagree, creating flipped triangles or invalid topology. Robust predicates evaluate a fast approximate determinant with an error bound; if the sign is certain they stop, and if uncertain they recompute with higher precision. This adaptive strategy spends extra work only near degeneracy. It does not make constructed intersection coordinates exact, but it protects discrete branching decisions that must be globally consistent in triangulation, mesh repair, and ray-edge intersection. Pose estimation, transforms, and robust fitting · Visibility queries and ray intersections · Meshes, connectivity, and geometry processing. Open Determinants orientation and volume in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: ODE initial-value problems and stiffness — ODE initial-value problems and stiffness Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism An ordinary differential equation specifies a state’s rate of change as a function of state and time. An initial-value problem adds the starting state; together they define the trajectory when existence and uniqueness conditions hold. Numerical integration advances approximate states through finite time steps. Stability concerns whether numerical errors remain controlled under repeated updates, not just whether one step is accurate. A stiff system contains modes with very different time scales; explicit methods may require impractically small steps to remain stable even when the visible solution changes slowly. Implicit methods can enlarge the stable step region but require solving equations. Consistency, stability, and convergence are distinct properties. A simulator should choose its step and integrator based on the dynamics, not merely the display frame interval or apparent smoothness of one trajectory. Prerequisites
Definite integrals and the fundamental theorem Eigenvalues and eigenspaces Absolute and relative error
Used by
ODE integration and stability Time integrators and symplectic updates
Full teaching explanation

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Screen-space ray generation and mouse picking — Screen-space ray generation and mouse picking Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11 Definition and mechanism A screen ray begins with a pixel location mapped through the viewport to NDC, then through inverse projection and camera pose into a world-space origin and direction. For perspective cameras, rays usually share the eye origin; orthographic rays have parallel directions but different origins across the image. Mouse picking must use the same high-DPI scaling, viewport offset, origin, and Y convention as rendering. Near and far unprojection can define a ray segment, but a point at infinity or an infinite far plane needs an explicit direction construction. Picking then intersects that ray with scene geometry or uses an object-ID buffer. Prerequisites
Camera view and clip-space pipeline Unit directions and safe normalization Visual angle and calibrated rays

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Spline bases and curve evaluation — Spline bases and curve evaluation Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism A spline is a piecewise polynomial curve whose neighboring pieces join under explicit continuity constraints. A cubic Bézier segment uses four control points and Bernstein weights; the weights sum to one, so the curve lies in their convex hull. A B-spline uses local basis functions so moving one control point changes only nearby spans rather than the whole curve. Knots mark where polynomial pieces meet; repeated knots reduce continuity. Catmull–Rom curves interpolate their control points and can be convenient for motion paths, while Bézier curves expose endpoint tangents through their handles. To evaluate a curve, compute basis weights at parameter <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>t</mi> </math> and take their weighted sum of control points. Position, first derivative, and parameterization speed matter separately: even a smooth path may speed up or slow down unless its parameter is adjusted. Prerequisites
Basis coordinates and dimension
Used by
Worlds, Images and Inference Bézier curves and De Casteljau evaluation Cubic Hermite interpolation ## Full teaching explanation

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Prefix scan and stream compaction — Prefix scan and stream compaction A prefix scan turns local counts into globally consistent offsets. For an exclusive sum scan of input <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>j</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>i</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </math> If each element says how many output records it will emit, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math> is the first output slot owned by element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>i</mi> </math>. This converts a race-prone global append into deterministic non-overlapping regions. For Boolean compaction, let predicate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>∈</mo> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo> </math>. Scan <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>b</mi> </math> to obtain offsets. Every active element with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math> writes itself to output[scan[i]]. The final output count is scan[n-1] + b[n-1]. Parallel structure The naive parallel scan that repeatedly doubles an offset performs <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mi>log</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> work. A work-efficient tree scan performs an up-sweep/reduction followed by a down-sweep and uses <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> work with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>log</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> depth. On a GPU, a practical large-array scan normally has several levels:
scan each workgroup block into local output; record each block total; scan the block totals; add each scanned block offset back into that block’s local results.
Every phase has a dependency. Dispatching all phases without establishing visibility/order is not a valid scan merely because each shader is individually correct. Shared-memory bank conflicts and subgroup width affect performance, while workgroup barriers only synchronize participating invocations in that workgroup. Stream compaction as an allocation proof Compaction is useful beyond filtering visible objects. It appears in GPU-driven draw generation, BVH construction, particle survival, tiled light lists, Gaussian tile duplication and sparse work queues. The scan proves that each surviving producer owns a distinct range before any scatter writes occur. Evidence boundary The current repository has CPU-side scan/compaction reasoning in the canonical volumes but does not yet claim a native Vulkan/Metal scan kernel benchmark. The next hardware proof should compare a scalar CPU oracle, a workgroup implementation, multi-workgroup hierarchy, adversarial non-power-of-two sizes, and captured GPU timing. Primary background: NVIDIA GPU Gems 3, Chapter 39, “Parallel Prefix Sum (Scan) with CUDA.” Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Scan turns local counts into nonoverlapping output regions. Related: GPU workgroups and synchronization, BVH build traversal and workload selection.. Open Prefix scan and stream compaction in Volume 1

For 0xAD, unsigned interpretation gives 173; eight-bit two’s complement gives −83. A contract must state width, signedness, field positions, byte order, allowed values, and any padding policy. Appendix.Content: This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Matrix norms and numerical error — Matrix norms and numerical error The spectral norm is the largest 2-norm stretch and equals the largest singular value. The Frobenius norm measures aggregate squared entry energy. Residuals, orthogonality errors, and condition numbers need a declared norm and scale; a small residual alone need not imply a sensitive solution is accurate. Use it when: setting scaled tolerances or interpreting numerical diagnostics. Developed in Phase 8: The spectral norm measures worst-case amplification, while the Frobenius norm accumulates squared energy across entries. The chapter uses them to scale residuals, reconstruction errors, and orthogonality defects, and separates backward error in a nearby problem from forward error in the requested answer. norms and scale · residuals and error interpretation Prerequisites Norms lengths and induced distances, Singular value decomposition, Forward and backward error. Used by Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse, Matrix functions, Sparse and iterative solvers. Teaching path: norms and error. A matrix norm can protect a geometry bound A local sphere under a linear transform is generally an ellipsoid. The Frobenius norm times its original radius gives a safe, possibly loose enclosing radius. Taking only the longest matrix column can fail under shear. The culling example derives the bound, demonstrates the shear counterexample, and links its geometric figure. This connects numerical matrix norms to conservative rejection decisions.. Open Matrix norms and numerical error in Volume 2

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Omnidirectional camera projections — Omnidirectional camera projections Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11 Definition and mechanism Cubemaps, equirectangular panoramas, and fisheye lenses map unit directions onto different image domains. A cubemap selects one of six faces and projects two direction components; equirectangular coordinates map longitude and latitude to a rectangle; fisheye mappings use a radial function of angular distance. These parameterizations are not equal-area: uniform pixel sampling does not imply uniform solid-angle sampling. Choose the mapping that matches capture or rendering needs, define face orientation and seam rules, and measure reconstruction with angular error between unit vectors. Fisheye formulas also differ (equidistant, equisolid, orthographic, stereographic), so name the model before interpreting pixels. At the poles, longitude is undefined, so seam and pole handling need explicit sampling rules. Prerequisites
Visual angle and calibrated rays Camera calibration and bundle adjustment Unit directions and safe normalization
Used by
No downstream concept node is added in this stage.
Full teaching explanation

The explicitly identified chunk groups remain M001–M010 and user-labeled M031–M036; the six new Phase 7 excerpts are not assigned unverified integrated-chunk identifiers. Part Supplied topic, expanded mechanism and narrative node 501 SCALARS AS ELEMENTS OF A NUMBER FIELD — Field laws make nonzero division and vector scaling meaningful; a floating type is only an approximation. Scalars fields and real-number models 502 REAL NUMBERS AND THE PROPERTIES GRAPHICS RELIES ON — Order, intervals and completeness justify real geometry; bounded machine values are not the complete number line. Scalars fields and real-number models 503 COMPLEX NUMBERS AND TWO-DIMENSIONAL ROTATION INTUITION — Unit complex multiplication rotates a plane; conjugation reverses it, and magnitude drift adds unwanted scale. Complex numbers and planar rotations 504 VECTORS AS GEOMETRIC DISPLACEMENTS — Free displacement survives translation of its starting point; location and movement are different roles. Vectors coordinates and affine points 505 VECTORS AS COORDINATE TUPLES — An ordered tuple gives components, but neither its basis nor physical role follows from storage shape. Vectors coordinates and affine points 506 THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN A VECTOR AND ITS COORDINATES — One physical vector has different coordinates in different bases; distinguish passive description from active motion. Vectors coordinates and affine points 507 VECTOR SPACES AND THEIR AXIOMS — Closure and vector-space laws enable consistent combinations; unit directions are a constrained non-example. Vector spaces subspaces and span 508 SUBSPACES — A nonempty subset closed under arbitrary two-vector combinations is a subspace; shifted planes need affine language. Vector spaces subspaces and span 509 LINEAR COMBINATIONS — Arbitrary coefficients generate movements, not necessarily averages; negative weights are valid. Vector spaces subspaces and span 510 SPAN — The span is the smallest subspace containing generators; redundant inputs do not enlarge it. Vector spaces subspaces and span 511 LINEAR INDEPENDENCE — A zero combination must have only zero coefficients for independence; near dependence is a numerical question. Basis coordinates and dimension 512 BASIS VECTORS — Spanning ensures reachability and independence ensures uniqueness; both are necessary for a basis. Basis coordinates and dimension 513 DIMENSION OF A VECTOR SPACE — Dimension counts basis elements over the selected field; a plane stored in three components still has dimension two. Basis coordinates and dimension 514 COORDINATE REPRESENTATION RELATIVE TO A BASIS — Coordinates weight an ordered basis; reconstruct the physical arrow before interpreting the tuple. Basis coordinates and dimension 515 CHANGING BASIS CONCEPTUALLY — Changing coordinates solves the new basis relation; near-parallel basis axes amplify coefficient uncertainty. Basis coordinates and dimension 516 STANDARD BASIS IN <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </math> — The two standard unit axes reconstruct every planar coordinate; visual up/right conventions remain separate. Basis coordinates and dimension 518 VECTOR ADDITION FROM THE PARALLELOGRAM RULE — Head-to-tail and parallelogram movement yield componentwise addition in a common basis. Part Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue 101 Translation units and linking — Source → preprocessing → semantic compilation → object/BMI → link. A declaration can permit compilation while an absent implementation fails linking; BMI is not object code. 102 Declarations and definitions — Every definition is a declaration, not conversely. extern int x declares; int x=0 defines. Forward class is incomplete; fixed-underlying opaque enum is complete. 103 One Definition Rule — Multiple translation units must describe coherent entities. Header guards are per-TU; ordinary external definitions and inline/template exceptions have different constraints. 104 Scopes and name lookup — Scope belongs to a name; qualified lookup selects a context; hiding changes lookup without deleting the hidden object. ADL adds associated candidates. 105 Storage duration and object lifetime — Automatic/static/thread/dynamic classify storage. A block-scope static outlives the block; a local pointer and its dynamic pointee have distinct durations. 106 Object construction and storage reuse — Sufficient aligned storage and completed initialization establish an ordinary object lifetime. destroy_at can end the object while the byte buffer remains; casts do not construct arbitrary objects. 107 Object identity and generation handles — Equal values need not be one object, and reused addresses host different occupants. A slot/generation needs live-registry validation, not merely a non-sentinel index. 108 Fixed-width integer types — sizeof(char)=1 C++ byte; CHAR_BIT≥8. int has minimum capacity, not a universal32-bit width. Exact/least/fast and size_t express different requirements. 109 Scoped enums and validated domains — Scoped enumerators and no implicit integer conversion reduce accidents. Explicit underlying width does not validate received codes; states and combinable flags need separate designs. 110 Aggregate initialization — C++20/23 aggregate criteria are not the older user-provided-constructor rule. Designators follow member declaration order. Braces may select initializer-list or ordinary constructors instead. 111 Class access and invariants — struct defaults members and bases public; class defaults them private. Both are class types. Record/invariant intent is convention, not a syntactic capability limit. 112 Standard-layout and trivial copyability — Alignment creates internal/tail padding. Traits do not imply array traversal, packing, serialization or GPU compatibility. Named x/y/z require explicit indexing or actual array storage.
